en: The Scripture on the Meritorious Adornments of the Buddha-field of the Great Sage Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Volume One.
By the Duke of Su, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, and Special Advancement.

[The monk] Bukong, who was granted a fief of three thousand households, invested with the purple robe, posthumously honored as Minister of Works, and given the title of Great Mirror, the Great Universal Wisdom of the Daixingshan Monastery, Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa, translated this by imperial decree: Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Bhagavat was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of one thousand bhikṣus;

and eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas, all of whom had attained non-retrogression from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, with Maitreya Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva as their leaders.
Furthermore, there were seventy-two koṭis of devas, all of whom dwelt in the vehicle of the bodhisattvas;
additionally, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, together with their retinues of forty thousand devas, were also all established in the vehicle of the bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, there were four asura kings—namely, the asura king Vemacitra, the asura king Māli, the asura king Kharaśiras, and the asura king Nandika—who were accompanied by hundreds of thousands of asura retinues.

Furthermore, there were sixty-two thousand great nāga kings, namely: the nāga king Nanda, the nāga king Upananda, the nāga king Varuṇa, the nāga king Manasvin, the nāga king Dharaṇīdhara, the nāga king Anavatapta, the nāga king Sumeru, the nāga king Mārapramardaka, and the nāga king Candrābha; these and others served as their leaders.

Furthermore, there were the Four Great Heavenly Kings—namely, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Virūḍhaka, Virūpākṣa, and Vaiśravaṇa—who were accompanied by hundreds of thousands of yakṣa retinues. These included the great yakṣas Kumbhīra, Aṭavaka, Sūciroma, Sumati, Vikṛtavigraha, Samantavigraha, and Acala, who served as their leaders.

At that time, the king and his ministers of Rājagṛha, as well as the fourfold assembly, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, non-humans, and others, each offered robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and various kinds of requisites to the Tathāgata with reverence and respect.

At that time, having accepted the King’s invitation for a meal, the World-Honored One dressed in the early morning and took up his bowl; surrounded by a multitude of bhikṣus and hundreds of thousands of devas and humans, he proceeded toward the palace of King Ajātaśatru in Rājagṛha.

By the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, he manifested great supernormal powers, emitting hundreds of thousands of kinds of wondrously colored light; hundreds of thousands of musical instruments played simultaneously, and a rain of various exquisite flowers—blue utpala, red padma, yellow kumuda, and white puṇḍarīka—fell down in profusion.

At that time, by the power of his supernormal faculties, the Tathāgata caused great jewel lotuses, as large as chariot wheels, to spring up wherever his feet touched the ground; they had stems of white silver and leaves of gold, with filaments made of vaidūrya gemstone, and within the calyx of each flower sat a manifested bodhisattva seated in the full lotus posture.
These bodhisattvas, together with jewel lotuses, circumambulated the city of Rājagṛha seven times, keeping it to their right, and spoke these verses:
“The caravan leader who benefits the world, The savior of sentient beings, the field of merit;
The Bull of the Śākyas, tranquil and of great majesty— The World-Honored One shall now enter this city.”
If there are those who wish to seek rebirth in heaven, Who seek liberation from the suffering of birth, old age, sickness, and death,
And who desire to conquer the armies of Māra, They should make offerings to the Lion of the Śākyas.
The name of the Muni is most difficult to hear; having practiced with diligence for many koṭis of kalpas, he brings benefit to the world out of compassion. Now the Great Sage enters this royal city.
For immeasurable and boundless eons he practiced giving—food, drink, clothing, and vehicles;
his beloved sons and daughters, as well as his wives; and he even relinquished his royal throne upon entering the city.
Able to give hands, feet, eyes, and ears, And relinquish the head, nose, and all other limbs,
By possessing the merit of total renunciation, One attains the supreme *sarvajñā* (omniscience).
Well-trained in the purity of the precepts of giving, supreme among men for his flawlessness in morality,
and endowed with the excellence of patience, he whose mind is tranquil now enters the city.
Having cultivated diligence for ten million eons, With weary detachment and compassion, he observes the world;
Entering meditative absorption and abiding in tranquility, The one with the Great Brahma-voice now enters the city.
Immeasurable wisdom is peerless, like space which has no bounds;
The merit of excellent patience and the precepts are likewise so; Such supreme practices are all utterly pure.
Through diligent valor, he has subdued the hosts of Māra; having attained immovable wisdom, he is free from sorrow and affliction.
Turning the subtle and wondrous Wheel of Dharma according to the teaching, the Great Dharma is now present as he enters the city.
Those who wish to seek me, the Sugata, adorned with the thirty-two marks,
and who have accomplished the practices and vows of the bodhicitta— such persons should go to approach and make offerings to me.
Having severed the afflictions of desire, hatred, and delusion, as well as other discursive thoughts and evil inclinations,
one should swiftly prepare immeasurable offerings and draw near to the Great Master.
If one desires to attain the state of Brahmā, Or that of Śakra, Lord of Devas, or Maheśvara,
With exquisite offerings and celestial music, One should make these offerings to the Great Muni.
If you wish to seek the status of a Wheel-Turning King over the four continents, attain the seven treasures,
and fulfill the vow of possessing a thousand sons who are all valiant, you should make offerings to the Honored One among Men.
Those who desire to become elders or minor kings, to obtain inexhaustible wealth and resources,
and to possess a countenance so upright and majestic that they surpass their kin— such persons should swiftly go to make offerings to the Muni.
If there are those who practice for liberation and delight in hearing the supreme Dharma of the Great Sage, you should go quickly to listen; what is difficult to hear has now been heard.

At that time, throughout the great city of Rājagṛha and its hundreds of thousands of villages and settlements, having been awakened by these verses, the men, women, boys, and girls therein each took up flowers, incense, burning incense, unguents, powdered incense, flower garlands, as well as gold and silver flowers, banners, pennants, conch shells, drums, horns, lutes, flutes, and various kinds of music. With single-minded contemplation, they prayed for the Buddha’s acceptance, leaping with joy and offering worship with reverence.

Then, as the World-Honored One was about to enter the city, he raised his right foot and pressed it upon the threshold of the city gate; the ground within the city shook in six ways. Hundreds of thousands of celestial and human musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck, and wonderful heavenly flowers rained down. All sentient beings within the city who were blind regained their sight, those who were deaf regained their hearing, the insane recovered their original minds, the naked obtained clothing, the hungry obtained food and drink, and the poor obtained wealth and resources.
At that time, they were likewise not oppressed by greed, hatred, delusion, stinginess, envy, anger, or pride; they looked upon one another with hearts of loving-kindness, like a father and son.
Within those musical sounds, a verse was spoken:
“The World-Honored One, endowed with the ten powers, has entered the city— This Great Man, the Lion of the Śākyas.
In an instant, all have attained great peace and happiness; The blind have gained their sight, and the deaf have gained their hearing.”
The insane regain their composure without distraction; those who are naked obtain clothing;
all who are hungry and thirsty receive food and drink; and the destitute obtain wealth and treasures.
Immeasurable devas in the void pay homage with reverence and offer praise.
Raining flowers as an offering to the Moon-like Tathāgata, with the sounds of drums, horns, conchs, and all manner of music, they were played in full as the Buddha entered the city.
Those who saw this marveled at its uniqueness and felt joy in their hearts; they were no longer oppressed by greed, hatred, or delusion.
Avarice, envy, pride, and all such [afflictions] were entirely eliminated; they looked upon one another with hearts of loving-kindness, like father and son.
When the Tathāgata, endowed with the ten powers, entered the city, the people were peaceful and happy, and all rejoiced.
Musical instruments sounded spontaneously without being struck, as they attained an extraordinary and supreme joy.

All this is through the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata; thus, the multitudes of devas, humans, asuras, and the world appear simultaneously in many such forms—extraordinary, most excellent, and inconceivable.
When the World-Honored One enters the city, he extensively performs deeds for the benefit of many people.

At that time, the World-Honored One entered the city of Rājagṛha. There was a lay bodhisattva mahāsattva, the son of a wealthy and noble elder named Vimalakīrti (Destroyer of Faults), who from afar in the midst of the lanes beheld the World-Honored One. His marks were extraordinary, his countenance was upright, serene, and clear; his faculties were tranquil, such that those who gazed upon him could never tire. He dwelt in the supreme subduing power of *śamatha*, guarding his sense-faculties like a well-trained elephant; his right mindfulness was undisturbed like a pure spring pool; and his body was adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics.

At that time, the bodhisattva, seeing that the Tathāgata’s physical marks were perfectly formed and majestic, gave rise to a heart of profound respect and pure faith; he then went to the Buddha’s presence, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Destroyer of Faults joined his palms in reverence before the World-Honored One and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

By accomplishing how many dharmas does a bodhisattva swiftly attain the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and in accordance with what they aspire for, purify a buddha-field and adorn a buddha-land?”
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, wishing out of compassion to crush their transgressions and knowing that the time for his transformative work had arrived, stood upon the main road.
At that time, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of people who all approached the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated at his feet, and stood with palms joined.
In the midst of the sky, there were again immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas who paid homage to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Bhagavān addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vinayaparicchedaka, saying:
"If a bodhisattva accomplishes one dharma, they will swiftly realize unsurpassed bodhi and, according to their aspirations, obtain a pure buddha-field."
What is this one dharma? Noble son!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should give rise to great compassion for all sentient beings and, with a superior intention, should resolve to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta.
What is the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*)? Good son!
As for the superior intention, once one has generated the bodhicitta, one should not give rise to even the slightest practice of unwholesome dharmas.
What is the practice of few unwholesome dharmas?
It means not practicing greed, not practicing anger, and not practicing delusion.
If one dwells as a householder, one’s deportment should not involve frivolous or playful conduct.

If one has gone forth from the household life, one should not seek honor or material gain, but should dwell well in the dharmas practiced by those who have gone forth—namely, the thorough realization of all dharmas as they truly are.
How does one thoroughly comprehend all phenomena as they truly are?
Noble son, "all phenomena" refers to the aggregates, the sense bases, and the elements.
How does one penetrate the five aggregates?

One should contemplate the five aggregates as being like an illusion—detached, empty, without objective referent, quiescent, and neither arising nor ceasing. To penetrate them in this manner, yet not perceive even one who penetrates them, is how one penetrates them.

There is neither seeing, nor knowing, nor thinking; there is neither discrimination nor that which is discriminated. To thoroughly penetrate the cessation of all discrimination is called the right practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who does not abandon sentient beings.
Why is this? Because he has personally realized those dharmas for himself; thus, for the sake of other sentient beings, he expounds that both sentient beings and dharmas are unapprehendable.
Son of good family!
"By the accomplishment of a single dharma, one will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and will thus be able to fully purify a buddha-field.

When this Dharma-gate for accomplishing the meritorious adornments of a buddha-field was spoken, the Bodhisattva Vighuṣṭaśabda attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Leaping for joy, he ascended into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees, and among that assembly, two thousand sentient beings resolved their minds upon awakening (*bodhicitta*).
Fourteen thousand devas and humans distanced themselves from dust and were freed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One smiled with serene joy; from his face, he emitted rays of light—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, purple, and so forth—which illuminated immeasurable and boundless worlds. Having shone upon them, the light returned, circled the Buddha three times, and entered through the crown of his head.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground,
and addressed the World-Honored One in verse: "O Sovereign of all dharmas who has reached the further shore, The Teacher of Ten Powers, the Most Supreme Honored One,
The All-Knowing One whose fame is heard throughout the world— I pray that you now explain the reason for your smile."
How does the Muni awaken to the past?
How does he fully awaken to the future?
And how does he perceive the present?
I pray that you explain the reason for your smile.
What are the mental activities of all sentient beings—their distinctions as inferior, middling, or superior?
Having liberated them from all conceptualizations and reached the further shore, O Tamer of Men, I pray that you speak the cause of your smile.
Billions of nayutas of devas have come, To pay homage to the World-Honored One with palms joined;
Within this great assembly they feel a thirst for the Dharma, And pray only that the Muni will preach the sublime teaching.
“Your wisdom has reached the further shore; no faults can be found in you.
You know all supreme practices—by what cause do you manifest a smile?
Thus, these billions of *koṭis* of devas who seek the Dharma,”
Immeasurable bhikṣus have all come to hear the True Dharma;
because they offer worship and make vows, with their immeasurable varieties of voices,
they all look up with longing, praying that the Buddha will dispel their doubts and delusions.
The Buddha said to the Venerable Ānanda,
"Do you now see this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vigata-dosa ascending into the air to a height of seven tāla trees?"
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
I have seen it.”
"Sugata, I have seen it.
The Buddha said:

“Ānanda! This Bodhisattva Vighuṣṭaśabda, after the passing of sixty-two hundred thousand asaṃkhyeya kalpas, shall attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) in this trichiliocosm during the Kalpa Free from Heat and Affliction (Vītasaṃtāpa), and he shall be known as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śāntavinīta-ghoṣa.”

Ānanda! The Buddha-field of that Tathāgata Śāntadāntasvara, with its meritorious adornments as well as its assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, is no different from the world-system Abhirati of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya.
At that time, having spoken this Dharma, the World-Honored One proceeded gradually from that place toward the palace of King Ajātaśatru.
Upon arrival, he and the assembly of bhikṣus each sat down in their respective order upon the prepared seats.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru, knowing that the Blessed One and the community of bhikṣus were seated, personally served various foods—possessing excellent color, fragrance, and flavor—to the Blessed One and the community of bhikṣus, providing for them until they were fully satisfied. He then offered exquisite garments to the Tathāgata and the assembly of bhikṣus, personally donning them upon the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
Having finished putting on his robes, he paid homage to the Buddha; then, withdrawing to one side and taking a low seat before the Buddha, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“From what do anger, resentment, concealment, as well as all faults and ignorance arise?
From what do they cease?
The Buddha told the Great King:
"Anger, resentment, concealment, and all manner of faults arise from 'I' and 'mine.
These notions of 'I' and 'mine' are established where nothing exists; not knowing virtues and defects is called ignorance."
If one knows "self" and "what belongs to self" as they truly are, neither knowledge nor ignorance can be conceptually established.
Therefore, Great King, you should train yourself in this way:
all conditioned phenomena are fundamentally without coming or going, and are beyond verbal expression.
"Great King!

Phenomena have no coming or going; phenomena that neither come nor go are neither born nor extinguished. That which is without birth or extinction is called wisdom, and this very absence of knowing is also called wisdom."
"Why is this? Because all phenomena enter and exit without mutual awareness; that which is without an object of knowledge is called wisdom.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How marvelous and extraordinary!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has so well expounded this. I would rather meet an untimely death while hearing the Dharma than live for a long duration without hearing it.”
At that time, the Great King again invited the World-Honored One to preach the Dharma during the late afternoon.
The World-Honored One immediately granted his consent.
Having finished the meal, he put away his robes and bowl, went to Vulture Peak Mountain, washed his feet, spread out his seat, and entered *samādhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One, desiring to preach the Dharma, arose from samādhi in the late afternoon.

Then the Venerable Śāriputra and all the great śrāvakas also arose from their meditative absorption; at that moment, the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī also arose from samādhi, accompanied by forty thousand devaputras.

The Bodhisattva Maitreya, together with a multitude of five thousand bodhisattvas, and the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāntagāminigarjitasvara, together with a multitude of five hundred bodhisattvas, all arose from their meditative absorption. Leading their respective retinues who surrounded them before and behind, they proceeded to Vulture Peak Mountain, prostrated themselves at the feet of the Buddha, and each having spread out a seat, withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru, surrounded by his retinue of attendants before and behind, went to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa to visit the Tathāgata; having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, there were also immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings in the city of Rājagṛha who all went together to Vulture Peak Mountain; having arrived at the place where the Tathāgata was, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, Śāriputra rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Just now, in the crossroads of the great city of Rājagṛha, the Tathāgata has briefly explained for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vinītapāpa the complete adornment of the meritorious qualities of a Buddha-field of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
Excellent, World-Honored One!

We pray that you will explain in detail how bodhisattvas practice the bodhisattva path so that they do not regress from unsurpassed enlightenment; how they attain all-knowledge and subdue Māra; how they defeat all non-Buddhists and purify all afflictions; how they adorn and purify buddha-fields and fulfill their vows; and how, having arisen with skillful wisdom, they transcend the stage of a Buddha to dwell in the stages of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; how they skillfully turn the wheel of Dharma and cultivate the pāramitās, enabling them to obtain the wisdom of sarvajñatā, manifesting as bodhisattvas to bring great benefit to immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings.

In this assembly, there are sons and daughters of good family who seek awakening; having had the opportunity to hear the sublime Dharma directly from the Buddha, they are filled with joy and exultation, and having rejoiced, they practice according to what has been taught.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"I shall now manifest such supernormal powers (ṛddhi) that the range of these manifested activities will pervade the ten directions."

He immediately emitted hundreds of thousands of rays of light; each ray of light produced hundreds of thousands of nayutas of rays within many Buddha-fields, illuminating those various lands and eclipsing the sun and moon. This radiance so overwhelmed the faculty of sight that the lights of all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, maṇis, lightning, and fire no longer appeared. Furthermore, the forms of the hells and the radiance of other sentient beings vanished entirely. Even the Cakravāḍa Mountains, Mahācakravāḍa Mountains, Mucilinda Mountains, Mahāmucilinda Mountains, Sumeru, the king of mountains, and all other black mountains, walls, and forests throughout the worlds of the ten directions were completely permeated by the illumination of the Buddha’s light.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had emitted this light, he made a sound of clearing his throat, awakening immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions.

At that moment, to the east of this world, beyond eighty-four *gaṅgā*-sands of Buddha-fields, there was a world named Universal Pervasiveness (*Samantavyāpin*). In that land dwelt a Buddha, titled Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śrīkūṭarāja, who currently resides in the world.

In that buddha-field, the names of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are not heard; it is filled solely with a pure assembly of great bodhisattvas. Each individual bodhisattva is surrounded by a retinue of one hundred koṭis of non-regressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, who stand before and behind them as their attendants.
In that world, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Dharmavīra.
For what reason was he named Dharmavīra?

When the Tathāgata Śrīkūṭarāja was teaching the Dharma amidst the assembly, the bodhisattva Dharmavīra, having heard the teaching, ascended into the air to a height of seven tala trees. Concealing his own body, he taught the Dharma for the sake of the assembly, namely the *dhāraṇī* of the Vajrapada from the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
At that time, the entire assembly thought to themselves:
"All dharmas consist of nothing but sound; why is it, noble son, that you do not see his body yet hear his voice?"
When such sounds emerged, form was accomplished yet did not appear;
as it was with form, so it was with sound;
as it was with sound, so it was with all phenomena.
Innumerable bodhisattvas attained forbearance; for this reason, he was named Dharmavīra.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmavīra, seeing a great radiance and hearing the sound of a cough, immediately went to the place of the Tathāgata Śrīkūṭarāja, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"For what cause and condition has there appeared in this world such a great radiance and the sound of a great clearing of the throat,
never before heard? Then,
the Tathāgata King of Auspicious Accumulation replied:

“Good son! To the west, passing from here through Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of eighty-four Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Sahā. There dwells a Buddha named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently resides in the world. Desiring to assemble koṭis of nayutas of bodhisattvas from the worlds of the ten directions to listen to the Dharma, he has emitted this light and the sound of his clearing his throat from all his pores.”
The Bodhisattva Dharmavīra then addressed the Tathāgata Śrīkūṭarāja, saying:
"World-Honored One!

I now wish to go to the Sahā world to pay homage, behold, make offerings to, and serve the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni; furthermore, I wish to see the assembly of bodhisattvas there and to hear the Dharma."
The Buddha said, “You may go; now is the very time.

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Dharmavīra, surrounded by a retinue of sixty koṭis of great bodhisattvas, vanished from that land and appeared within this realm in the time it takes a strong man to flex and extend his arm.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmavīra had this thought:
"By what kind of supernormal power (ṛddhi-vidhi) shall I now go there to pay homage, visit, and make offerings to the Tathāgata Śākyamuni?"

Having formed this thought, he immediately entered the *samādhi* of Universal Adornment (*sarvavyūha*). By the power of the supernormal knowledge of the realm of phenomena (*ṛddhividhi*) resulting from this *samādhi*, he caused this trichiliocosm to be filled with exquisite flowers piled up to the knees; hundreds of thousands of musical instruments played simultaneously, and it was adorned with various precious banners, pennants, and canopies. Furthermore, exquisite fragrances were universally diffused throughout this world, making it resemble the palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods.

At that time, after the Bodhisattva Dharmavīra had manifested his supernatural powers, he went together with the other bodhisattvas to the place where the Tathāgata Śākyamuni was. He prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and then, by the power of his vows, manifested a lotus flower in the direction from which they had come and sat upon it.

At that time, ninety-six koṭi-nayuta buddha-fields away from here to the south, there was a world named Free from Dust. There currently resides a Buddha named Siṃhavikrāntagāmin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is respectfully surrounded by a great assembly of immeasurable bodhisattvas.
In that world, there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Ratnapāṇi (Jewel-Hand). For what reason is he called Jewel-Hand?

It is because when that bodhisattva transforms sentient beings in various buddha-fields, he reaches out with his right hand and touches as many buddha-worlds as he desires, accomplishing whatever he intends. From his hand issue the sounds of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; the sounds of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity; and the sounds of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of other various dharma-jewels. For this reason, he is called Jewel-Hand.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ratnapāṇi, seeing a great radiance and hearing the sound of a cough—such as he had never before heard or seen—went at once to the presence of the Tathāgata Siṃhavikrāntagāmin and, prostrating his head at the Buddha’s feet, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"For what cause and condition has this auspicious sign appeared— a great radiance— and is this sound of such a great coughing heard?
The Buddha said, "Good son!

To the north, passing from here through ninety-six *koṭi-nayuta* Buddha-fields, there is a world named Sahā. There dwells the Buddha Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently resides there. He emits great radiance from all his pores and makes the sound of a cough in order to proclaim the meritorious adornments of that Buddha-field, so as to cause countless bodhisattvas to each take up the adornments of their own original vows for a Buddha-field; it is for this reason that he manifests this auspicious omen.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi again addressed the Tathāgata Siṃhavikrāntagāmin, saying:
“I now wish to go to the Sahā world to pay homage to, visit, make offerings to, and serve the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, as well as to see the various bodhisattvas and hear the Dharma.”
The Buddha said,
"What need is there to go to that world of defilement?
Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what purpose and benefit did the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni perceive that he took up that defiled world rather than a pure buddha-field?”
The Buddha said,
"Good son! That Blessed One,
the World-Honored One, spoke these words in the distant past, throughout the long night:”

“May I swiftly attain the accomplishment of great compassion, and always, amidst sentient beings who are corrupt and evil, realize unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma.
Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi again addressed the Tathāgata Siṃhavikrāntagāmin, saying:
“World-Honored One!

That Tathāgata Śākyamuni was indeed able, in the past, to make this great and difficult-to-utter vow of compassion to appear in such a world of evil; such a Benevolent Honored One is extremely rare to encounter, and I shall now go to pay him homage and behold him in person.
The Buddha said, “You may go; now is precisely the right time.

However, as you approach him, you must observe with great care and prudence so as not to injure yourself. Although that Buddha and his Bodhisattvas are difficult to encounter, other sentient beings have dispositions that are treacherous and crooked, making them difficult to tame.”
The Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Although that land may have anger, resentment, and enmity, it shall not harm me. Even if all sentient beings were to harbor hatred and revile me for as long as the future endures, throughout koṭis of kalpas—even if they were to strike and hurl at me with knives, staves, tiles, or stones—I would endure it all and never retaliate.”
Then the Tathāgata Siṃhavikrāntagāmin addressed the entire assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
"Sons of good family!
If you are able to don the armor of patience just as the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi has done, you may go together with him to the Sahā world."

After the Tathāgata Siṃhavikrāntagāmin had spoken these words, the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, with single-minded concentration, surrounded by immeasurable bodhisattvas from that assembly, vanished from that realm and appeared in this world-system.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi thought to himself:
"By what range of supernormal powers shall I now pay homage to the Tathāgata Śākyamuni?
How may I bring peace and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings?"

Having formed this thought, he immediately manifested the sphere of supernatural power (*ṛddhi-viṣaya*), covering this trichiliocosm with his right hand. From his hand, he rained down various foods, drinks, garments, and vehicles, as well as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, pearls, conch shells, coral, and jade, completely fulfilling the hopes and aspirations of all sentient beings according to their hearts' desires.

To those who delighted in hearing the Dharma, he caused them to hear the Dharma from his hand; furthermore, he enabled immeasurable sentient beings who heard the Dharma to realize the truth through direct realization (*sākṣātkriyā*), and also caused countless sentient beings to experience supreme and wondrous bliss.

At that time, having manifested such a realm of supernatural power, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ratnapāṇi, together with the other bodhisattvas, went to the place where the Tathāgata Śākyamuni was. He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and then, by the power of his vows, manifested a lotus flower according to the direction from which he had come and sat upon it.

At that time, to the west of here, beyond ninety koṭi-nayuta-hundred-thousand buddha-fields, there was a world named Ratnagarbha. In that land there was a Buddha, titled Ratnakūṭarāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently resides there.

That Buddha-field is pure, being composed of vaidūrya; it contains no śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but only a host of pure great bodhisattvas. As they come, go, sit, or stand upon the vaidūrya ground, they all clearly behold the Tathāgata Ratnākara manifest before them, just as one sees the reflection of one's own face in a clear, bright mirror.

In that same manner, these bodhisattvas behold the Buddha, the World-Honored One, within those lands; having beheld him, they request the Dharma, and the Buddha then expounds for them his former original vows. Upon hearing this Dharma, those bodhisattvas attain patience (*kṣānti*).

That Tathāgata Ratnakūṭarāja constantly emits a great radiance from the maṇi-jewel within the tuft of hair between his eyebrows, which illuminates that entire land. The light of the sun and moon is completely eclipsed so that day and night cannot be distinguished; day and night are discerned only by the opening and closing of flowers.

At that time, within the realm of the Tathāgata Ratnākara-rāja, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Viśiṣṭapraṇidhijñāna. Encountering the radiance of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni’s touch and hearing the sound of his coughing, he immediately went to the presence of the Tathāgata Ratnākara-rāja. Prostrating with his head at the Buddha’s feet, he withdrew to stand to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"For what cause and condition, within this world, do such sounds of coughing and great radiance appear?
The Buddha said, "Good son!

To the east, passing from here through ninety *koṭi-nayuta* hundreds of thousands of Buddha-fields, there is a world named Sahā. There, the Buddha is named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Desiring to assemble *koṭi-nayuta* bodhisattvas from the worlds of the ten directions so that they may hear the Dharma, he emits great rays of light from all his pores and utters a sound like a cough.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Viśiṣṭapraṇidhijñāna, having heard these words, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I now wish to go to the Sahā world in order to pay homage to, behold, make offerings to, and serve the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni, and also to see those bodhisattvas there and hear the Dharma.”
The Buddha said, “You may go; now is precisely the right time.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Viśiṣṭapraṇidhijñāna, together with the various bodhisattvas, arrived at the Sahā world in a single kṣaṇa.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Viśiṣṭacāritramati had this thought:
"By what kind of supernatural transformation shall I now go there to pay homage to the Tathāgata Śākyamuni?"

Having formed this thought, he entered into samādhi. By means of the supernormal power of the divine realm (*ṛddhividhi*) resulting from this samādhi, he caused all the sufferings of the animal realm, the *yāma* hell, and the realm of Yama within this trichiliocosm to cease entirely. In a single instant, they attained unsurpassed and supreme bliss, and the fires of the hells were completely extinguished. All sentient beings in the realms of hungry ghosts, animals, and Yama obtained full satisfaction for their hunger and thirst; in that very moment, they attained peace and happiness, just like a bhikṣu who has entered the first dhyāna.

At that time, there was not a single sentient being who was oppressed by greed, hatred, or delusion; nor by anger, resentment, malice, or harm; nor by stinginess, pride, envy, or jealousy; nor by deceit, hypocrisy, or concealment. All sentient beings throughout every realm of existence gave rise to hearts of loving-kindness and altruism toward one another.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Viśeṣacāritramati, having manifested such supernormal powers of the realm of miracles, went together with the other bodhisattvas to the presence of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni. He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and then, by the power of his vow, manifested a lotus flower in the direction from which he had come and sat upon it.

At that time, sixty-three thousand Buddha-fields away from here in the northern direction, there was a world named Constantly Adorned; a Buddha currently resides there, titled King Born of the Śāla Tree.
In that world, there are no householders wearing secular clothing; all bodhisattvas wear the kāṣāya.

Furthermore, even the name "woman" is unheard of in that world, let alone those born from a womb; everyone wears the robes of the kāṣāya and is born by transformation upon lotuses in the full lotus posture.
That Buddha, the World-Honored One, constantly expounds for the sake of all bodhisattvas the Dharma-gate of the Seal of Nature (*dharmamudrā*).
What is meant by the Dharma-gate of the Seal of Nature?

It refers to the generation of the bodhicitta, which constitutes the fulfillment of the bodhisattva vows (*vinaya*) and serves as the fundamental locus for entering the *dhāraṇī* of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.

Because the mind is undistracted and capable of practicing equanimity, one enters the samādhi of emptiness; because one abides in right practice, one enters the samādhi of signlessness; because there is no expectation, one enters the samādhi of wishlessness.

Because the nature is free from desire, one penetrates the aggregates, sense bases, and elements, attaining awakening regarding objects of expectation; yet, regarding the Buddha’s wisdom, there is no arising of formal vows. Thus, one penetrates all phenomena, severing all conceptualization and non-conceptualization regarding all phenomena.
Because they hold such a view, it is called the Dharma-gate of the Seal of Nature (*dharmamudrā*).

In that assembly, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named King of the Constellation Accumulation Adorned with Marks (*lakṣaṇavyūhajātarājā*), whose original vows were sublime: if any sentient being beheld his body, they would certainly attain the thirty-two marks.

At that time, that bodhisattva, encountering the Buddha’s radiance and hearing the sound of his coughing, went to the place where the Tathāgata King Born of the Śāla Tree resided. He prostrated at the Tathāgata’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"For what cause and condition do these great lights and the sound of clearing one's throat appear?
That Buddha replied,
"O son of good family!"

To the south of here, beyond sixty-three thousand buddha-fields, there is a world named Sahā. There dwells a Buddha, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni, who emits this light from all his pores and makes this sound of clearing his throat, desiring to assemble the great bodhisattvas from countless worlds throughout the ten directions so that they may hear the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva King Accumulated with Constellations Adorned with Marks said:
“By what causes and conditions is this world named Sahā?
The Buddha replied:
"That world is able to endure greed, anger, ignorance, and all manner of suffering and affliction; therefore, it is named the Sahā World.
The Bodhisattva King of the Accumulated Constellations Adorned with Marks said, "Do all the sentient beings in that Sahā World truly endure being reviled, abused, and beaten?"
The Buddha said, “Good son!
Among the sentient beings in that buddha-world, few are able to accomplish such merit; rather, most follow along with greed, anger, delusion, resentment, and the fetters of bondage.”
That bodhisattva said,
"If that is so, that world should not be named Sahā.
The Buddha said:
“Lakṣaṇavyūha-tārā-rājasamudgata!

In that buddha-field, there are also sons and daughters of good family who practice the bodhisattva vehicle; they have already made offerings to immeasurable buddhas and have accomplished patience. They protect sentient beings and skillfully discipline themselves; even if sentient beings come to harm them with various instruments of suffering, they are able to endure it all, never giving way to negligence, greed, anger, or delusion.”
"Good son! Because there are such virtuous beings as these, that realm is named Sahā.

Furthermore, within the world of that Tathāgata Śākyamuni, there are also sentient beings who are fully possessed of manifold evils and rarely repent; their minds are coarse and wild, lacking shame and remorse, and they do not revere the Buddha, do not honor the Dharma, and do not love the Saṅgha—they shall fall into the hells, the animal realm, or be born as hungry ghosts."

That Tathāgata Śākyamuni, amidst these inferior sentient beings, is able to fully endure abuse, contempt, resentment, slander, harassment, harsh words, and enmity; his mind is like the great earth, immovable and unyielding. Whether he receives offerings or does not receive them, his mind is without fluctuation, neither exalting nor degrading, and free from both hatred and affection. For this reason, that realm is named Sahā.
At that time, the Bodhisattva King Accumulated Constellations Adorned with Marks addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We have now obtained great and excellent benefit, for we were not born among those wretched, evil, and inferior sentient beings.”
The Buddha said:
"Good son, do not speak in this way."

Why is this? To the northeast there is a world named Thousand Adornments, where a Buddha currently resides, known as Mahesvararaja Tathagata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha. The sentient beings in that land are all fully endowed with uniform peace and happiness; their bliss is just like that of a bhikṣu who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).

If sentient beings were to practice the various pure conducts (*brahmacarya*) in that buddha-field for a hundred *koṭis* of years, it would not equal the merit obtained by giving rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward sentient beings here in this Sahā world for even the duration of a finger-snap; how much more so if one can abide in a pure mind for a single day and night!
At that time, the Bodhisattva King Constellation-Accumulation-Adorned-with-Marks addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We wish to go to the Sahā world in order to pay homage to, visit, make offerings to, and serve the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni, and furthermore to see those bodhisattvas there and hear the Dharma.”
The Buddha said, “You may go; now is precisely the right time.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva King Samalaṃkṛtaketudhvaja, together with a hundred koṭis of bodhisattvas, vanished from that land and arrived in the Sahā world in a single kṣaṇa.
At that moment, the Bodhisattva King of the Accumulation of Constellations (Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña), adorned with his marks, had this thought:
"By what power of supernormal faculties shall I now make offerings, pay homage, and visit the Tathāgata Śākyamuni?"

Having formed this thought, by means of his own supernormal power of the base of psychic mastery (*ṛddhividhi*), he manifested a jeweled canopy in the midst of space that covered this trichiliocosm. Hundreds of thousands of millions of pearl necklaces and jeweled banners hung down all around it, and from within that canopy, various kinds of flowers rained down; hundreds of thousands of musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck.

Furthermore, he caused the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others in this assembly to each see themselves, endowed with the thirty-two marks, appearing within the precious canopy.

At that time, the Bodhisattva King of the Accumulation of Constellations Adorned with Marks, having performed such miraculous powers, went together with the other bodhisattvas to the place where the Tathāgata Śākyamuni was. He prostrated at the Tathāgata’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and by the power of his vows, manifested a lotus flower in the direction from which he had come and sat upon it.

In this manner, throughout the ten directions, in each of the immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* Buddha-fields, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* bodhisattvas, upon seeing the great radiance and hearing the sound of coughing, all asked their respective World-Honored Ones and came to this land. Having prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet, they likewise sat to one side; it was just so for everyone.

Furthermore, within this trichiliocosm, the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, as well as Śakra, Brahmā, the World-Protectors, and other deities of great majesty and power, all beheld the radiance and heard the sound of his clearing his throat; they all came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had manifested such supernatural powers, all the bodhisattvas who had gathered from incalculable, koṭi, immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of nayutas of Buddha-fields in the ten directions beheld the magnificent adornments of merit of this land, as well as the physical dimensions of the Buddha and the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, and their respective articles of use; each was exactly equal to those in their own lands. Each and every bodhisattva perceived his own body to be situated therein.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, and knelt with his right knee on the ground. Joining his palms toward the Buddha, he spoke in verse:
"Your boundless wisdom is heard throughout the ten directions; Your great light shines universally upon the realms of humans and devas.
Though all sentient beings together should attempt to measure it, No one is able to fathom the Buddha’s wisdom."
Bodhisattvas from the ten directions, immeasurable in number, have all gathered here for the sake of seeking the Dharma;
dwelling here, they all gaze upon and revere the Buddha, thirsting with longing for the Great Muni.
The Tathāgata, endowed with morality, concentration, and wisdom, is majestic and fearless like a lion;
his light of wisdom shines like the sun across the void, and his renown is heard throughout all Buddha-fields.
The devas, nāgas, and spirits, together with men and women, as well as the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, all join their palms in reverent homage;
may the Buddha, out of compassion, preach the Dharma for them.
Those who are to be liberated in the past, present, and future, you know with certainty to be vessels for the Dharma;
the Tathāgata well understands all sentient beings—may you please expound [the teaching] to dispel our doubts.
How do the sons of the Buddhas practice so as to attain pure lands free from dust and defilement?
How do they fulfill their great vows?
O Tathāgata, please explain this to me in detail.
How is it that one is not stained by stinginess?
How is it that one does not violate the precepts?
How is it that one can cross over while being subjected to insults and humiliation?
Can you endure being reviled, abused, and slandered?
How can you be so courageous and diligent in your vigor, practicing without weariness for tens of millions of kalpas?
How can you cause all sentient beings, who suffer immeasurable afflictions, to attain great peace and happiness?
How does one focus the mind with constant equanimity, abiding in samādhi with a pure heart,
so as to remain unstained by all sensory objects, just as a lotus is not wetted by water?
How can one preach the profound Dharma and attain the supramundane wisdom?
How can one subdue the armies of Māra and ultimately realize unsurpassed enlightenment?
The Sūtra on the Meritorious Adornments of the Buddha-field of the Great Sage Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Volume One;
The Sūtra on the Meritorious Adornments of the Buddha-field of the Great Sage Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Volume Two.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Da Xingshan Monastery—Kai-fu-yi-tong-san-si, Te-jin, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Duke of Su with a fief of three thousand households, recipient of the purple robe, posthumously honored as Minister of Works, and titled Dajian (Great Mirror), with the honorary name Dayangzhi (Great and Vast Wisdom)—by Imperial Decree. At that time, the Tathāgata addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya, saying:

“You shall now prepare a Dharma-seat for the Buddha; once I have ascended it, I shall proclaim the various practices cultivated through my past aspirations, the skillful means for generating the merit and adornments of all Buddha-fields, and the Dharma-gate for proceeding toward correct practice.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya had this thought:
"For what reason does the World-Honored One now command me to prepare the seat,
rather than having Ānanda, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, or others do so?"
Why do you set aside those śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas? Is this not taught solely for the purification of bodhisattvas?
Or is it because those śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are not vessels for this dharma-gate, and thus you have had me prepare the seats for the sake of the bodhisattvas?

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya immediately manifested the sphere of supernatural powers. By means of these powers, he conjured a lion throne four thousand *yojanas* high, adorned all around with immeasurable jewels and spread upon it with celestial, exquisite garments. Those garments were so soft that anyone who touched them attained peace and happiness. From that throne, various kinds of light radiated forth, illuminating this trichiliocosm.
At that time, the Tathāgata rose from his original seat and ascended this throne; the trichiliocosm shook in six ways in a manner unlike any ordinary occurrence.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Śāriputra:
"If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will be able to fulfill all their aspirations."
What are the four?
First, the aspiration to set out for enlightenment;
second, giving rise to a heart of compassion toward all sentient beings.
Third, the arousal of diligence.
Fourth, drawing near to spiritual friends.
By accomplishing these four dharmas, a bodhisattva fulfills their great vows.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva accomplishes one dharma,
they will not retreat from their great vow and will achieve the purification of a buddha-field.
What is this one dharma that a bodhisattva should study?
When the Tathāgata Akṣobhya was a bodhisattva, he originally practiced and made this great vow, saying:
"In whatever place I may be born, if I do not renounce the household life, I would be deceiving the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions."

"In this way, Śāriputra, these bodhisattvas should train accordingly; whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, they shall all certainly renounce the home for the homeless life in every place of birth."
Why is this? Because for all bodhisattvas, the most supreme benefit is what is called renunciation. Śāriputra!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who delight in leaving the household life are able to acquire ten kinds of merit. What are these ten?
First, they are not attached to any sensual desires.
Second, delighting in the aranya;
third, practicing what the Buddhas have practiced;
fourth, not being attached to wife and children, nor craving wealth and profit.
Fifth, the dharma of abandoning conduct leading to evil destinies;
sixth, the dharma of practicing conduct leading to auspicious destinies;
seventh, being able to attain the accomplishment of roots of goodness.
Eighth, they accumulate roots of goodness without ever falling away from them.
Ninth, they are constantly praised by all the devas.
Tenth, they are always protected by non-human beings.
Śāriputra! Those who delight in leaving the household life are able to acquire these ten kinds of merit. Therefore, Śāriputra!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who seek perfect enlightenment and who wish to liberate sentient beings, therefore always delight in leaving the household life.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
This is called the accomplishment of one dharma: not retreating from the great vow and attaining a pure Buddha-field according to one’s own wishes.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
When a bodhisattva accomplishes two dharmas, they do not regress from their great vows and purify buddha-fields according to their aspirations. What are these two? They are as follows:

the bodhisattva does not delight in seeking the state of a śrāvaka, does not delight in seeking the śrāvaka vehicle, does not take pleasure in the teachings spoken by śrāvakas, does not delight in associating with those of the śrāvaka vehicle, does not train in the śrāvaka’s code of discipline, does not delight in proclaiming doctrines corresponding to the shared śrāvaka vehicle, nor does he encourage others to practice the śrāvaka vehicle.
It is likewise with the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas;
it is solely for the purpose of exhorting and inspiring sentient beings to achieve the supreme, unsurpassed *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is called the second.
Śāriputra! If there is one who encourages others to enter the Buddha Vehicle, this bodhisattva will be able to acquire ten kinds of merit.
What are these ten?
First, to encompass buddha-fields that are free from śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
second, to obtain a purely singular assembly of great bodhisattvas;
third, to be protected and remembered by all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
Fourth, they are constantly praised by name by all Buddhas, who preach the Dharma for them.
Fifth, they give rise to a vast and expansive mind regarding all matters.
Sixth, if they are reborn in the heavens, they shall become Śakra or Brahmādeva.
Seventh, if born among humans, one becomes a wheel-turning sage king (*cakravartin*).
Eighth, one constantly beholds the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and is never separated from them.
Ninth, one is cherished and delighted by all devas and humans.
Tenth, they attain an indestructible retinue and an immeasurable accumulation of merit.
Why is this? Śāriputra!

If there were one who could cause all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm to attain the fruit of Arhatship or the stage of a Pratyekabuddha, and another who could establish even a single sentient being in the Bodhi of a Buddha, the merit of the latter would far exceed that of the former.

Why is this? Śāriputra, if śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas were to appear in the world, they would not be able to ensure that the lineage of the Buddha remains unbroken; yet, if a Buddha-Tathāgata does not appear in the world, there are likewise no śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Śāriputra! Because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, appears in the world, the lineage of the Buddhas is able to remain unbroken; thus, there are the designations of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Śāriputra! By thus exhorting others to abide in the bodhicitta, one obtains these ten kinds of merit: one does not retreat from the great vow, and one attains a pure Buddha-field according to one’s own aspirations.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva accomplishes three dharmas,
they will not retreat from their great vow and will grasp the meritorious adornments of the buddha-fields.
What are these three?
First, to dwell with reverence in an araṇya;
second, to practice the gift of Dharma without expectation of reward;
third, to abide securely in the discipline of pure precepts.
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva abides in the discipline of pure ethical conduct, they are able to obtain ten kinds of fearlessness. What are these ten?
First, fearlessness in entering a village;
second, fearlessness in preaching the Dharma among the assembly;
third, fearlessness regarding food and drink.
Fourth, fearlessness in leaving the village;
fifth, fearlessness in entering the monastery;
sixth, fearlessness in entering the assembly of monks.
Seventh, sitting peacefully without fear;
eighth, approaching one's preceptor (upādhyāya) and teacher (ācārya) without fear;
ninth, instructing the great assembly while abiding in a mind of loving-kindness without fear.
Tenth is the fearlessness regarding the use of clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other requisites for life. "Śāriputra,
by abiding securely in the discipline of pure ethical conduct, one attains these ten kinds of fearlessness."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva teaches the Dharma with a mind free from expectation, they are further able to acquire ten kinds of merit. What are these ten?
First, not to be possessed by excessive desire;
second, not to seek recognition from others; third, not to seek fame.
Fourth, the mind does not become attached to the households of donors.
Fifth, one does not covet disciples from noble families.
Sixth, one gives rise to contentment regarding both coarse and fine things.
Seventh, when the devas come to visit him, he does not give rise to pride.
Eighth, he does not regress from the mental attention directed toward the contemplation of the Buddha.
Ninth, the teachings he proclaims are accepted with faith by others.
Tenth, they give rise to the mind that recollects the Buddha. Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva practices the gift of Dharma with a mind free from expectation, they obtain these ten kinds of merit.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva honors and dwells in an araṇya, they are further able to accomplish ten kinds of merit. What are these ten?
First, to distance oneself from useless talk;
second, to delight in tranquility;
third, to have the mind focused on a state of meditative concentration.
Fourth, not engaging in worldly affairs;
fifth, loving and revering all Buddhas;
sixth, not abandoning the joy and bliss of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Seventh, when practicing the holy life, there are no obstacles.
Eighth, with little application of effort, one realizes samādhi.
Ninth, the collection of names, phrases, and syllables of the teachings received is never forgotten.
Tenth, they fully comprehend the meaning of all the teachings they have heard. Śāriputra,
by dwelling in an araṇya with reverence, a bodhisattva attains these ten kinds of merit.
If a bodhisattva accomplishes three dharmas, they will not regress from their great vow and will attain a pure buddha-field according to their wish.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will not retreat from their great vows and will attain a pure buddha-field according to their aspirations.
What are these four?
First, speaking truthful words and practicing according to what one has said.
Second, they are always humble and self-effacing, eliminating all conceit.
Third, they remain far removed from stinginess and envy.
Fourth, when seeing others in prosperity and glory, their hearts give rise to joy.
These are called the four dharmas that one accomplishes. Furthermore, Śāriputra,
there are four kinds of merit in a bodhisattva’s truthful speech.
What are the four?
First, his mouth constantly emits the fragrance of blue lotuses.
Second, his verbal karma is pure and his speech is unimpeded.
Third, they serve as the standard and measure for humans and devas.
Fourth, they encompass the perfect vocal resonance of all Buddhas. Śāriputra!
“A bodhisattva who speaks truthful words attains these four kinds of merit.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, there are four kinds of merit for a bodhisattva who is humble.”
What are the four?
First, one distances oneself from the evil realms and does not take birth in the bodies of various animals, such as camels, donkeys, oxen, horses, or dogs.
Second, one is not subjected to contempt or disparagement.
Third, evil friends and enemies cannot assail them.
Fourth, they are constantly venerated and prostrated to by humans and devas. Śāriputra!
This is how a bodhisattva, through humility, attains these four kinds of merit.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, there are four kinds of merit for a bodhisattva who remains free from stinginess and envy.
What are the four?
First, not forgetting the mind of renunciation.
Second, acting as a great donor during times of famine.
Third, one should never keep the doors closed.
Fourth, upon seeing those who observe the rules of discipline (*vinaya*), one should not give rise to envy regarding giving or receiving. Śāriputra!
This is how a bodhisattva, by remaining far removed from stinginess and envy, attains these four kinds of merit.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva sees the prosperity of others and gives rise to a heart of joy, there are four kinds of merit.
What are the four? First, one should constantly give rise to this thought: "For the sake of those sentient beings, I shall don this armor so as to bring them happiness;
once they have obtained wealth and treasures through their own merit and by their own power and thereby enjoy peace and bliss, may it cause me redoubled joy."
Second, all their wealth and possessions cannot be seized by kings, nor by water or fire, nor by bandits or evil associates.
Third, wherever they are born, they will be fully endowed with riches, treasures, sons, daughters, and retinues; even emperors will rejoice in them, let alone other people.
Fourth, their wealth and treasures are vast, and they enjoy them inexhaustibly. Śāriputra,
these are the four kinds of merit that a bodhisattva obtains by feeling joy in his heart upon seeing the prosperity of others.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva accomplishes five dharmas,
they will not retreat from their great vow and will attain a pure buddha-field according to their wish.
What are these five?
First, a bodhisattva should seek the Dharma for the sake of purifying buddha-fields and accomplishing their adornments; having heard that Dharma from others, they should inquire:
"How does a bodhisattva accomplish such adornments of merit?"
"Having heard this, one should practice according to what has been taught and immediately seek to realize the true mark of *tathatā*.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, secondly, when a bodhisattva wishes to make a vow to be born in a pure buddha-field, they should maintain pure ethical discipline (*śīla*). Because their discipline is pure, they will certainly be born in accordance with their vow. Once born in that pure buddha-field, they should observe that land and take note of its characteristics: the various adornments, the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, and the requisites enjoyed by the great assembly. Having grasped these characteristics, they should develop deep reverence, join their palms, and approach the Buddha to inquire about the Dharma."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Thirdly, when a bodhisattva takes up the merit and adornments of those vast buddha-fields, that Buddha, the World-Honored One, knowing his superior intention, immediately expounds them for him."
"By virtue of the Buddha’s teaching, they are able to accomplish the magnificent adornments of merit of vast buddha-fields; having heard the Dharma, they practice according to the instructions.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
Fourth, the bodhisattva brings both phenomena (*vastu*) and wisdom (*jñāna*) to purity, remaining far removed from what is not the Dharma (*adharma*).
What are phenomena? What is wisdom?
Because it is free from the wisdom of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas regarding the subjective perceiver and the objective perceived, it is called "wisdom" (jñāna);
because one practices all the teachings as they have been heard, it is called "activity" (vastu).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Fifth, a bodhisattva knows the self-nature of the Buddha and knows the self-nature of the buddha-field.
What is the self-nature of the Buddha?
What is the intrinsic nature of a buddha-field?
Both the Buddha and the buddha-field exist as nothing more than names; knowing that these names are pure, one does not give rise to attachment because of such knowledge.
In this way, Śāriputra,
it is by accomplishing these five dharmas that a bodhisattva does not retreat from their great vow and attains a buddha-field whose purity accords with their aspirations.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes six dharmas, they swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and transcend all worlds to take up a pure buddha-field."

What are the six? First, this bodhisattva acts as a great donor and practices relinquishment; regarding all cherished and beloved precious objects and the like, he feels a sense of shame [at attachment] and is able to give them away entirely, leaping with joy and reflecting:
"I practice the great gift to fulfill the Great Vehicle; I shall bring supreme enlightenment to completion."
He further thought: "One cannot attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment by means of such a small portion.
Having reflected thus, he gave away all his prosperity and wealth; he should even give away his own body and life, let alone other property, wife, children, or grandchildren.
For what reason?
Śāriputra, as for "sarvajñatā" (all-knowledge), what is its meaning?
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the bodhisattva path, he relinquishes everything he possesses; for this reason, he attains awakening, which is called "omniscience" (sarvajñatā).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Second, whether they be lay bodhisattvas or ordained bodhisattvas, if they abide in the discipline of pure ethical conduct (*śīla-saṃvara*), they shall never, even for the sake of their livelihood, violate the disciplinary rules (*saṃvara*) upheld by the precepts of pure ethical conduct. They dedicate the merit of this commitment toward all sentient beings, and they experience great joy upon attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

"I am one who upholds the precepts; I have conceived a deep love for the pure discipline of the Vinaya. Day and night I exclusively cultivate the blissful Brahma-faring, whereby the Buddha-dharma manifests before me. In accordance with principle, I attain the contemplation of the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Abiding in this contemplation of the true nature, I attain profound patience (*kṣānti*); by realizing this profound patience, I attain right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*). By virtue of right view, I practice correctly; by abiding in correct practice, I develop revulsion toward the three realms (*tridhātu*). Through revulsion for the three realms, I give rise to fear;

through fear, I seek liberation. With the vision of liberation in mind, I form this thought: 'Since I am subject to such suffering and affliction, all sentient beings must likewise be so. I should take up this heavy burden on behalf of those sentient beings, so that they may attain ultimate peace and happiness.'"

"When one performs such contemplation, one immediately attains great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); having abided in great compassion, one arouses great vigor (*vīrya*), exerting oneself with such urgency as if one's head or clothing were on fire, never relinquishing that vigor, whereby one is able to attain the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*)."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Thirdly, a bodhisattva should don the armor of patience, free from arrogance, and attain the power of great forbearance; when encountering verbal abuse or physical assault, they shall achieve patience and give rise to no resentment."
One should reflect thus:

"Even if there were a club as large as Mount Sumeru, and someone were to seize it to strike me, or even if I were constantly subjected to harsh abuse for a full *koṭi* of eons, I should not give rise to a mind of anger or resentment."
Why is this? Those sentient beings have not yet followed the Buddha’s training, whereas I desire to train as a Buddha and Bodhisattva.
Therefore, whatever beating or abuse they may inflict will only serve to increase my great compassion accordingly.

I shall don the armor of the great vow for the sake of those sentient beings, gathering them in so that they may attain liberation, depart from birth and death, and enter into nirvana; therefore, I ought not to harbor anger or resentment now.
"If one is clad in such armor of patience, one will immediately attain ten kinds of accomplishments. What are these ten?
First, the accomplishment of noble lineage."
Second, the accomplishment of wealth and property;
third, the accomplishment of retinue and kin;
fourth, the accomplishment of physical appearance and characteristics.
Fifth, the accomplishment of relinquishing through generosity;
sixth, the accomplishment of spiritual friends;
seventh, the accomplishment of hearing the true Dharma.
Eighth, the accomplishment of practicing according to the teachings.
Ninth, at the time of death, the accomplishment of seeing and serving the Buddhas.
Tenth, having seen the Buddhas, the accomplishment of giving rise to pure faith.
“Śāriputra! These are the ten kinds of accomplishments of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!”
Fourth, the Bodhisattva generates great diligence and makes firm and essential vows to accomplish wholesome dharmas. Donning such armor of diligence, they reflect:

"For the sake of each and every sentient being, until the end of the future, I shall practice all forms of diligent conduct within the cycle of birth and death in succession, never becoming weary, through the excellence of my vows."

"For the sake of all sentient beings, I shall undergo the cycle of birth and death for as many eons as there are, exerting such diligence as never to abandon them. Śāriputra, if there were a bodhisattva who,

with the seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in each of the ten directions, offered these to the Tathāgata at every moment of thought, continuing in this manner until the end of the future;
If there is a bodhisattva who, inwardly harboring a superior intention and dwelling in a mind of great compassion, dons the armor of diligence with such a mind, this merit is even greater than that.
Śāriputra! A bodhisattva who possesses this diligence attains ten kinds of merit.
What are these ten?
First, to remain free from the conduct of the foolish and worldly;
second, to embrace the conduct of the Buddhas;
third, to perceive the cycle of birth and death as a source of suffering and affliction.
Fourth, by this one embraces great compassion.
Fifth, one does not retreat from former original vows.
Sixth, one has few illnesses.
Seventh, because they do not transgress against the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time;
eighth, because their lust, anger, and delusion are attenuated;
ninth, because they thoroughly penetrate all names, phrases, and syllables according to what they have heard.
Tenth is the accomplishment of spiritual practice. Śāriputra,
those who exert diligence obtain these ten kinds of merit.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Fifth, a bodhisattva recollects the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; by this means, the mind attains focused concentration upon the Tathāgata, constantly achieving the meditative stabilization of tranquil mindfulness."
He reflects thus: "I should practice the conduct of a Tathāgata;

if my mind is distracted or loses mindfulness, I shall not attain the supreme state, which is the wisdom of a Buddha. Therefore, I should relinquish all things grasped by the mind, and likewise abandon all gain, honor, villages, cities, food, drink, requisites for life, and all kinsmen and friends. Yet, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, I shall not abandon them; I shall delight in dwelling in an araṇya, a place of tranquility, wandering alone without companion like the single horn of a rhinoceros."

Having dwelt in a secluded place such as an araṇya, one gives rise to a mind of great loving-kindness (*maitrī*), first pervading one direction, then the second, third, and fourth, and finally the ten directions; dwelling in this mind of loving-kindness universally toward all sentient beings, once so established, one is called a practitioner who dwells in *dhyāna*.

Śāriputra! Suppose there were a bodhisattva who, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, were to provide all manner of articles of enjoyment to as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, along with their assemblies of bhikṣus and their retinues.
If there is an ordained bodhisattva seeking tranquility who goes to an araṇya and walks seven steps, the merit of this is far greater than that. Why is this?
Because one can thus swiftly attain great enlightenment. Śāriputra,
those who delight in tranquility and dwell in dhyāna will obtain ten kinds of merit.
What are the ten? First, attaining mindfulness;
second, attaining wisdom.
Third, attaining correct practice;
fourth, firm resolve and courageous vigor;
fifth, attaining swift eloquence.
Sixth, they attain dhāraṇīs.
Seventh, they attain skillfulness regarding birth and death.
Eighth, they remain unshakable in the aggregate of ethical discipline and so forth.
Ninth, all devas serve them.
Tenth, they do not covet the prosperity and glory of others. Śāriputra!
Those who delight in dwelling in tranquility and practicing dhyāna obtain these ten kinds of merit. Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Sixth, the bodhisattva should skillfully understand that which flows forth from wisdom and form this thought:
"From what does wisdom arise?

It arises from the state of pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*). Furthermore, this wisdom can cause all wholesome dharmas (*śukla-dharma*) to increase; therefore, the bodhisattva should study all worldly wisdom."
He thoroughly studied all arts, incantations, and medical prescriptions—those difficult to perform and difficult to master. Having studied these, he further thought:
"Yet this wisdom cannot lead to the realization of the tranquil extinction that is free from desire, nor can it lead toward the supernormal powers or perfect enlightenment."

"It does not lead toward the state of a śramaṇa, nor toward that of a brāhmaṇa, nor toward nirvāṇa; therefore, I must now further seek everywhere for the skillful means of the medicine of the Dharma, so that through such wisdom I may attain that ultimate tranquility."

Thus, that bodhisattva seeks the source of all phenomena and does not perceive even the slightest phenomenon capable of giving rise to other phenomena. Because he does not perceive them, he abides in quiescence; because he abides in quiescence, he is free from feverish affliction; being free from feverish affliction, he thoroughly understands birth and death, and acts for the benefit of sentient beings, causing all sentient beings to extinguish their manifold sufferings.
"Śāriputra! These are the six dharmas by which a bodhisattva achieves non-retrogression from their great vow and attains a buddha-field according to their heart's desire.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
When a bodhisattva accomplishes seven dharmas, they do not regress from their great vow and attain a pure buddha-field according to their wish. What are the seven?
First, they relinquish everything they possess, because that which is relinquished cannot be apprehended.
Second, they are unimpaired in their ethical discipline because they do not conceptualize ethical discipline.
Third, they are patient and gentle because sentient beings cannot be apprehended.
Fourth, they initiate diligence because body, speech, and mind cannot be apprehended.
Thus, fifth, he accomplishes meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), because he does not abide in meditative concentration.
Sixth, his wisdom is perfected, because it is free from conceptual discrimination (*avikalpa*).
Seventh, he recollects all Buddhas, because he is far removed from signs (*nimitta*).
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva thus accomplishes these seven dharmas, they do not regress from their great vow and attain the various adornments of all pure buddha-fields.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva accomplishes eight dharmas,
they will not regress from their great vow and will attain a pure buddha-field according to their wish.
What are these eight?
First, the mind is free from envy;
second, one gives ornaments; third, the mind is vast.
Fourth, to honor and respect the Dharma teacher;
fifth, to refrain from wrong livelihood;
sixth, to practice impartial giving.
Seventh, not being self-conceited;
eighth, not disparaging others. Śāriputra!
These are the eight dharmas by which a bodhisattva accomplishes the non-retrogression of their great vows and attains a buddha-field as pure as they desire.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes nine dharmas, they do not regress from their great vow and attain a pure buddha-field according to their aspiration.
What are these nine?
First, they possess physical restraint.
Second, they possess restraint of speech.
Third, they possess restraint of mind.
Fourth, they cause craving and desire to wither away.
Fifth, it causes hatred to subside;
sixth, it causes delusion to subside;
seventh, one does not engage in deception.
Eighth, to be a steadfast and virtuous friend.
Ninth, not to treat a virtuous friend with contempt or arrogance. Śāriputra!
When a bodhisattva thus accomplishes these nine dharmas, they do not regress from their great vows and attain a pure buddha-field according to their aspirations.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they will not regress from their great vows and will attain a pure buddha-field according to their wishes. What are these ten?
First, when a bodhisattva takes up exquisite flowers and goes before a Tathāgata or a stūpa to perform an offering, they make this vow, saying:
“Such exquisite flowers as these possess such superior color and fragrance that all who see them rejoice.
