When I attain Buddhahood, may my Buddha-field be strewn everywhere with various wonderful flowers, and may it be adorned on all sides by trees made of various jewels, including burning incense, powdered incense, and ointment incense; and when clothing, food, drink, jeweled canopies, banners, and pennants, as well as treasures such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, pearls, musaragalva, and coral are offered in homage, they too should be dedicated in this way toward the adornment of the Buddha-field.
A Bodhisattva should abide in pure ethical discipline; for one who abides in the precepts, whatever they wish for in their heart shall be accomplished.”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra! Second, when a bodhisattva observes his own experience of happiness, he makes this aspiration:
'May others also share in such happiness together with me.'
"Therefore, when a Bodhisattva attains perfect enlightenment, all sentient beings within that Buddha-field shall be fully endowed with uniform peace and happiness.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
Third, a bodhisattva does not utter unpleasant words toward others, but always speaks with skillful speech.
They make this aspiration:
"When I attain enlightenment, may no sentient beings in my buddha-field hear unpleasant sounds, but may they always hear sounds that are pleasing to the mind."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra! Fourth, a bodhisattva constantly exhorts sentient beings to cultivate the ten paths of wholesome action, and together with all sentient beings, dedicates all roots of goodness toward the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), [vowing]:
'When I attain enlightenment, may all within my buddha-field fully accomplish the ten paths of wholesome karma.'"
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, fifthly,

wherever a bodhisattva goes, regarding all sentient beings— whether men, women, boys, or girls— whom they see with their eyes, they exhort them all to cultivate unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, never praising the fruits of the two vehicles."

Therefore, when a bodhisattva attains enlightenment, all sentient beings born within that buddha-field will universally resolve their minds toward unsurpassed bodhi, remain far removed from the inclinations of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and shall obtain such a pure land, filled with a multitude of bodhisattvas.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, sixth, a bodhisattva never obstructs the gains and offerings of others; seeing others obtain gain, they always give rise to joy."

Therefore, when a bodhisattva attains enlightenment, all sentient beings within that buddha-field will enjoy an uninterrupted supply of necessities and provisions, and they shall obtain such great illumination of the Dharma.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, seventhly,
if a bodhisattva sees a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī who has committed an offense, he never reveals it, but dwells instead solely within the True Dharma."
Therefore, when a bodhisattva attains enlightenment, there shall be no sound of fault whatsoever in that buddha-field.
Why is this? Because the entire great assembly has attained the dharma of purity and freedom from fault.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, eighthly, a bodhisattva delights in the Dharma and seeks the Dharma without giving rise to feverish distress; whatever Dharma they hear, they dwell correctly in its practice."

"When he attains awakening, within that buddha-field, sentient beings who delight in the Dharma will be free from all feverish affliction and shall practice in accordance with the Dharma as they have heard it.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

Ninth, when a bodhisattva offers various musical instruments—such as conch shells, drums, horns, strings, and pipes—to a Tathāgata’s stūpa, they dedicate these roots of goodness toward the accomplishment of the adornments of a buddha-field.
Therefore, when a bodhisattva attains awakening, hundreds of thousands of musical instruments in that buddha-field will resound spontaneously without being struck.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Tenth, if a bodhisattva sees sentient beings who have lost mindfulness, they make this vow:
"May they attain right mindfulness.
For this reason, when that bodhisattva attains bodhi, all sentient beings within that buddha-field shall subsist on the food of dhyāna-joy.
“Śāriputra! Such a buddha-field is endowed with such merit that even if the Tathāgata were to speak of it with his eloquence for an eon, or more than an eon, he could not exhaust its description.”

Śāriputra! Nevertheless, I shall now speak briefly according to the inclinations of these bodhisattvas, so that those with superior resolve, having heard this, will proceed toward it and attain the perfect merits of a buddha-field.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva accomplishes three dharmas,
they will swiftly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and all the Buddha-fields they seek will be fully realized."
What are the three dharmas?
First, abiding in heedfulness.
Second, initiating correct practice in accordance with the Dharma as it has been heard.
Third, they give rise to sublime great vows.

"Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva accomplishes these three dharmas, they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and they will attain the fulfillment of all pure buddha-fields according to their aspirations."
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
It is rare indeed that the Tathāgata has so excellently expounded this Dharma."

"Bhagavān! By dwelling in heedfulness, one obtains all factors conducive to enlightenment; by dwelling in correct practice, one attains great enlightenment; and by the excellence of great vows, one accomplishes a buddha-field."
The Buddha told Śāriputra: “So it is, so it is!

Just as you have said, it is through heedfulness that one attains the factors of enlightenment; by abiding in correct practice, one attains great awakening; and by giving rise to sublime and great vows, one attains the complete adornment of a pure buddha-field.”
Śāriputra! Just as I, in the past, by relying on supreme vows, accomplished such a buddha-field. Śāriputra!
Because I dwelt in heedfulness, I fulfilled my original vow; because I practiced correctly, I attained great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*). Śāriputra!
If one merely speaks without practicing, one cannot even reach the stage of a śrāvaka, let alone attain unsurpassed enlightenment.
Therefore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva should resolve upon truth, practice according to what they have spoken, and train in the various points of training in this manner.
At that time, forty thousand bodhisattvas within the assembly rose from their seats, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and with one voice said to him:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, I shall train myself in the bodhisattva precepts, dwelling in heedfulness to accomplish their practice, fulfilling my great vows and purifying the buddha-fields.
"I shall practice such conduct as this; whatever vows these bodhisattvas may have, I shall fulfill them.
At that time, the World-Honored One smiled with a serene countenance. Then Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what reason and by what cause do you manifest this smile?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Do you see these sons of good family making this lion's roar?"
Śāriputra replied, “Indeed, I have seen them.
The Buddha said:

“Śāriputra! After hundreds of thousands of kalpas, these sons of good family will each attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in different lands, all sharing the same name, Praṇidhāna-vyūha (Adorned by Vows). They will be just like the future Buddha Siṃha and others; their lands will be pure, neither superior nor inferior to the land of the Tathāgata Amitāyus, with the sole exception of the length of their lifespans.”
Śāriputra asked, "What is the lifespan of those Tathāgatas?
The Buddha said:
“Each of those Buddhas has a lifespan of ten kalpas.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāntagajagarjitasvara rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta Bodhisattva is constantly praised by all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
How long will it be before this Mañjuśrī attains unsurpassed bodhi?
"What will the Buddha-field that you shall attain be like?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Siṃhavikrāntagāminigarjitasvara, saying: "Good son!..."
"You should ask the Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta Bodhisattva yourself.
Then the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāntagāminigarjitasvara addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"At what time will you attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
He replied: "Good son! Why do you not ask me how one dwells in unsurpassed bodhi?"
Yet you ask me about attaining *bodhi*. Why is this?
Since I do not even abide in *bodhi*, how could I be made to realize *bodhi*?
"The Dharma of Bodhi neither abides nor is it realized; how then could I have anything to realize or abide in? Siṃhavikrama said, "Mañjuśrī!"
"Do you not seek to realize bodhi for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings? He replied, "No!"
Good son! Why is this?
Because sentient beings cannot be apprehended.
If sentient beings were to exist as something to be apprehended, I would have realized awakening for their sake and remained in awakening.
Since sentient beings, life-span, and the person (*pudgala*) are all non-existent, I therefore neither abide in awakening nor do I regress from it.
Siṃhavikrama said: “Mañjuśrī! Do you not abide in the Buddha-dharma?”
"No, son of good family!
All dharmas abide within the Buddha-dharma; whatever dharmas there may be are untainted, boundless, signless, and formless. Therefore, the Buddha abides in Suchness."
"Just as the Buddha abides, so too are all dharmas. Siṃhavikrama spoke again: "Good son!..."
As for what you have now said—that I do not abide in the Buddha-dharma—I shall now inquire into this matter; you should grant me your forbearance and explain it to me.
He replied: "Good son, what do you think?"
Do you seek awakening for the sake of form?
Do you seek awakening for the intrinsic nature of form, for the suchness of form, for the self-nature of form, for the emptiness of form, for the detachment of form, or for the dharma-nature of form?
"Good son! What do you think?
If form were bodhi, would form then realize bodhi?"

“Is it by means of the intrinsic nature of form, the suchness of form, the self-nature of form, the emptiness of form, the detachment of form, or the dharma-nature of form that one realizes awakening? He replied, “No!”

Mañjuśrī! Form does not seek awakening; awakening is formless, its original nature is formless, suchness is formless, its self-nature is formless, emptiness is formless, detachment is formless, and the dharma-nature is formless, yet one realizes awakening. This is explained at length, up to: even the dharma-nature of form does not realize awakening.
Mañjuśrī said: "Good son, what do you think?"
"Is awakening sought through feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness?
Son of good family!
Is awakening realized through feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness?"
"Is it by realizing the dharma-nature of even consciousness that one attains bodhi? He replied, "No!"

Mañjuśrī! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not seek awakening, nor do they realize awakening; even the dharmic nature of consciousness does not seek awakening, nor does it realize awakening.
Mañjuśrī said: "Good son, what do you think?"
“Is there a designation of a self or what belongs to a self apart from the five aggregates? He replied, “No!”
Mañjuśrī said: “Good son, how can one realize bodhi through two dharmas?”
Siṃhavikrama said, “Mañjuśrī!
When bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds hear such words, they all give rise to fear and trepidation toward Mañjuśrī, taking these words of Mañjuśrī as the definitive standard.”
These bodhisattvas spoke these words:
"I do not seek awakening; I do not realize awakening. Mañjuśrī said:

“Good son! All dharmas are without fear, and within the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) there is likewise no fear. The Buddha teaches the Dharma for those who are without fear; if one is fearful, then aversion arises;
if aversion arises, then desire is abandoned.”
If one is free from desire, one is liberated;
if one is liberated, there is no bodhi;
if there is no bodhi, this is non-attachment.
If one is without attachment, then there is no going;
if there is no going, then there is no coming;
if there is no coming, then there is no seeking or wishing.
If there is no aspiration or seeking, then there is nothing to be sought;
if there is nothing to be sought, then there is no regression;
if there is no regression, from what could one regress?
Does he regress from the grasping at a self?
Or does he regress due to the conceptualization of signs and distinctions regarding the arising of the notions of permanence or annihilation concerning sentient beings, life-span, and the *pudgala*?
If he were to regress, how could there be regression for one who is non-regressive?
Do they regress from emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the limit of reality, and the various Buddha-dharmas?
From what Buddha-dharma do they regress?

It is said that they do not depart from the Buddha-dharmas, nor do they reach their ultimate consummation therein. They are without objectification and without entry or exit; they are without activity and without indication. They exist only as names. They are empty, unarisen and unceasing, neither going nor coming, far removed from both purity and defilement, free from dust and detached from dust, neither uneven nor unequal, far removed from mental application, inexhaustible and without attachment, neither equal nor unequal—this is what constitutes the Buddha-dharmas.
"Good son! All Buddha-dharmas are this dharma of non-dharma. Why is that?
Because that location cannot be apprehended.
If the Buddha-dharma were to arise in such a manner, O son of good family!
A bodhisattva who has newly resolved upon enlightenment, having heard this teaching, would feel awe and fear and would swiftly realize bodhi.
"If one does not feel alarm or fear, one will not realize bodhi. Siṃhavikrama said, "Mañjuśrī!..."
"How is it that you speak with such intentional meaning? He replied, "Good son!"
Whether they experience fear or conceptualization, they all realize awakening.
Whether they have thus resolved their minds or have not so resolved, those who seek perfect enlightenment will all realize awakening.

Furthermore, those who do not resolve their minds toward enlightenment shall not attain it; nor do they contemplate it, for that bodhicitta is in reality unattainable. Nor do they engage in conceptual discrimination, and if they do not engage in conceptual discrimination, they do not realize perfect awakening.
For what reason do they not realize perfect enlightenment?
They do not attain bodhi, nor do they realize bodhi. Why is this?
"Good son! Does the realm of space realize bodhi? He replied:
"No," Mañjuśrī said, "O son of good family!"
"Does the Tathāgata not say that all dharmas are identical to empty space? He replied, "So it is, so it is!"
Mañjuśrī! As it is said that space is such, so too is bodhi; as is bodhi, so too is space.
"Space and bodhi are non-dual and without distinction.
If a bodhisattva knows this equality, then there is nothing known, nor is there anything unknown.
When this Dharma was spoken, fourteen thousand bhikṣus exhausted all outflows and attained liberation of mind.
Twelve *nayuta* of bhikṣus were distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena;
ninety-six thousand sentient beings, who had never before resolved upon unexcelled bodhicitta, now all did so;
and fifty thousand bodhisattvas attained the forbearance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāntagāminirghoṣa addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"How long has it been since you first resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta?"
Mañjuśrī said: "Stop, son of good family!"
Do not give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding dharmas that are non-arising. Good son!
If there should be one who speaks thus:
"I have generated the bodhicitta; I am practicing for the sake of bodhi"—those who speak thus are holders of great false views.
O son of good family!

“I do not perceive that mind as having been generated for the sake of bodhi; because the mind is unperceivable, I have therefore not generated the mind for the sake of bodhi. Siṃhavikrāṇḍa said: “Mañjuśrī!
"What is the meaning of this phrase? Mañjuśrī replied, "Good son!..."
"If there is nothing seen, this is called equality, as was just explained. Siṃhavikrāṇta said: "Mañjuśrī!..."
"What is meant by 'equality'? "Good son! Equality is the absence of manifold characteristics.

Because of this equality, it is said that all dharmas have a single flavor (*ekarasa*). That which has a single flavor is called 'one nature' (*ekadhātu*); that which is called one nature is the nature of quiescence (*śāntatā*), wherein there is neither defilement nor purity."
Thus he teaches the Dharma—neither annihilated nor eternal, neither arising nor ceasing, without self and without grasping, neither taking up nor rejecting;
thus he teaches the Dharma, and having taught it, there is nothing to be thought and nothing to be discriminated.
"Good son! To give rise to the wisdom of practice within this dharma of equality is called 'equality.
Furthermore, good son!"
When a bodhisattva enters into such a dharma-nature, seeing neither difference nor unity, it is called equality.
That which is equal is free from inequality; within both inequality and equality, it is fundamentally pure.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāntagāminirghoṣa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Now Mañjuśrī is unwilling to speak for himself regarding how far back my aspiration for unexcelled bodhi was first conceived; the great assembly all desire to hear this.”
The Buddha said, “Good son!

Mañjuśrī is one who possesses profound patience (*kṣānti*). Even this profound patience cannot be apprehended; awakening (*bodhi*) cannot be apprehended, and the mind (*citta*) cannot be apprehended either. Because the mind cannot be apprehended, for this reason I do not speak of the distance or proximity of the arousal of the mind.”
"Good son! You should listen attentively; I shall now speak.
The youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī has long since resolved his mind upon unsurpassed bodhi."

“Good son! In the distant past, more than seventy million *asaṃkhyeya* hundreds of thousands of *gaṅgā*-sands of *kalpas* ago, there was a Buddha named Ghoṣadatta Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, who appeared in the world. To the east, passing beyond seventy-two *nayuta* of Buddha-fields from here, there was a world named Ajāta; therein, that Tathāgata Ghoṣadatta preached the Dharma. Among his assembly of śrāvakas, there were eighty-four *koṭi-nayuta*, and the assembly of bodhisattvas was twice as many as that.”
“Good son! At that time there was a king named Ākāśa, who possessed the seven treasures and ruled over the four continents; governing by means of the True Dharma, he was a Wheel-Turning King.”

"Good son! That King Ākāśa, within the assembly of the Tathāgata Garjitasvara, for eighty-four thousand years provided various musical instruments, clothing, food and drink, palaces, towers, and pavilions—each of these being exceptionally exquisite—as well as male and female servants and attendants, to reverently make offerings to and serve the Tathāgata Garjitasvara, along with the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas. His royal kinsmen, the ladies of the inner court, the princes, and the ministers were solely devoted to making offerings and did nothing else. Although many years passed, he never felt weary. After those eighty-four thousand years had elapsed, the king was then dwelling alone without companions and reflected thus:
'I have already accumulated immeasurable roots of goodness; toward what aspiration should I now dedicate these roots of goodness?'"
Is it to seek the status of Śakra?
Or that of a Brahmā king?
Or that of a Cakravartin wheel-turning sage king?
"Is it for the sake of seeking the vehicle of the śrāvakas or the pratyekabuddhas? "Good son!
After that King of Space had thought this, the devas in the sky addressed him, saying:"
"Great King! Stop! Stop!"
Do not give rise to such inferior thoughts. Why is this?
The mass of merit accumulated by the King is exceedingly vast; Great King, you ought to resolve upon unsurpassed bodhicitta.
"Good son! At that time, having heard these words, King Ākāśa was filled with joy and thought to himself:
'I shall now certainly never retreat from this.'"
"Why is this? It is because the deva knew my mind and has come to inform me. "Good son!

At that time, the King of Space, together with eight hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of sentient beings, went to the place where the Tathāgata Thunderous Sound resided; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and withdrew to sit at one side.
Furthermore, noble son!
That King of Space joined his palms toward the Tathāgata Thunderous Sound and spoke these verses:
"I ask concerning the most supreme Dharma; I only pray that the Honored One among Men will explain it."
How does one attain supremacy, becoming a great man, the most honored among men?
Before the World-Honored One, I have made extensive offerings;
yet with a mind free from dependence, I have never before performed a dedication of merit.
Dwelling in solitude, this thought arose: "With a single-pointed focus, I bind my mind thus:
'I have already performed vast merit; how shall I dedicate it?
Is it for the sake of seeking the status of Śakra or Brahmā, or that of a Wheel-Turning King?'"
"Is it for the sake of seeking the state of a śrāvaka, or even that of a pratyekabuddha?
As such thoughts arose in my mind, the devas addressed me, saying:
"If you give rise to an inferior mind, your merit shall be destroyed."
“Great King, you have made a supreme vow to bring benefit to all sentient beings;
for the sake of delivering the world, you should give rise to the bodhicitta.
Thus I questioned the All-Knowing One, the Sovereign of all Dharmas:
"How does one give rise to this mind and achieve equal and perfect enlightenment?
By what means is this state attained? Please reveal this to me:
how should one give rise to the thought of bodhi so as to become equal to the Muni?"
Hearing these words from the sky, I have thus addressed the Tathāgata:
"Great King, you should know that I shall now explain in due order how all phenomena belong to causes and conditions, with desire as their root."
Just as they have aspired, so too shall they obtain the fruit.
In the past, I too once gave rise to this mind;
for the benefit of all sentient beings, I made such a supreme vow.
By virtue of that supreme vow, one attains an extraordinary fruit;
I have realized great Bodhi and fulfilled my sublime aspirations.
Great King, you should be courageous and give rise to such a mind.
"And by practicing this sublime conduct, you will surely attain perfect enlightenment.
Hearing these words from the Buddha, the king was filled with great joy;
he let out a lion’s roar, causing the entire world to tremble:
"From the very beginningless limit, until the end of the bounds of birth and death,
for the benefit of all sentient beings, I shall practice boundless conduct.
Before this great assembly, I have awakened the bodhicitta."
I vow to deliver all living beings, so that they may all be free from manifold sufferings.
From this day forward, may I never harbor defilements,
such as anger, malice, or envy, nor the pride of self-conceit or craving for sensory pleasures.
This would be a deception of the Buddhas of the ten directions and those of the present.
From this moment until the realization of Bodhi, I vow to practice the Brahma-faring; I renounce the fault of craving.
Following the Buddha in my practice, I shall cultivate pure precepts, gentleness, and patience;
without a hurried mind, I shall swiftly seek to attain perfect enlightenment.
Throughout the entirety of the future, toward every single sentient being,
Purifying Buddha-fields, immeasurable and inconceivable, Proclaiming their names so that they are heard throughout the lands of the ten directions— I now bestow upon myself this prediction:
That you shall attain Buddhahood; of this there should be no doubt.
In the presence of the Teacher, I purify my mental karma,
and I purify my physical karma, as well as my verbal karma;
I shall bring them all to complete purity and shall not give rise to what is unwholesome.
By my practice of truth, I have attained Buddhahood to benefit the world.
By virtue of these words of sincerity, the earth shall tremble in six ways;
if my speech were not true, the four great elements would shift and change from their positions.
Because of the truthfulness of their words, various musical instruments shall spontaneously play in the air.
Furthermore, they shall be free from all fetters and afflictions; it is because of this truthfulness that this occurs.
May celestial wondrous flowers rain down;
because of this true awakening, immeasurable koṭis of lands throughout the ten directions tremble.
A hundred million musical instruments played, raining down exquisite *māndārava* flowers as high as Mount Meru.
Twenty *koṭis* of people followed that king in their studies, all producing subtle and wondrous sounds:
"We shall attain Buddhahood"—
just as these twenty koṭis [of beings], so too shall all people likewise learn from the King and seek perfect enlightenment.
“Good son! Do not view King Ākāśa of that time as anyone else; he is none other than the present Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta Bodhisattva! At that time, the Kumārabhūta Bodhisattva was King Ākāśa.

Having passed seventy million *asaṃkhyeya* hundreds of thousands of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* kalpas, he first gave rise to the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). Furthermore, after passing sixty *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* kalpas, he attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). From that point onward, he fulfilled the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and perfected the ten powers (*daśabala*); he also fulfilled all the stages of the Tathāgatas and fulfilled all Buddha-dharmas, yet never for a single thought-moment did he give rise to such a mind [of self-conceit].”
"I have realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, noble son, those twenty *koṭis* of people who, together with that king, had resolved their minds toward enlightenment in the presence of the Tathāgata Ghoṣadatta, have all already realized unsurpassed enlightenment and turned the irreversible wheel of Dharma. They have performed the Buddha-work for incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings, and having completed that Buddha-work, they have entered parinirvāṇa through the nirvāṇa of a Buddha.

They were all inspired by Mañjuśrī; they have all successively served [the Buddhas] in generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and they have fully upheld the teachings of all those Buddhas.

There is another Buddha remaining here in this lower direction, beyond forty Ganges-sands of buddha-fields. The world is named Earth, and the Buddha’s name is Earth-Deva. His lifespan is immeasurable, and he currently dwells in the world, surrounded by an infinite assembly of śrāvakas.
When this account of Mañjuśrī’s past deeds was spoken, seven thousand sentient beings within the assembly all resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Scripture on the Meritorious Adornments of the Buddha-field of the Great Sage Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Volume Middle;
The Scripture on the Meritorious Adornments of the Buddha-field of the Great Sage Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Volume Lower.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Monastery—Great Master of Universal Wisdom, posthumously titled Great Mirror, who was invested with the rank of Kai-fu-yi-tong-san-si, Te-jin, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Duke of Su Commandery with a fief of three thousand households, granted the purple robe, and ennobled as Minister of Works. At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāntaghoṣa addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Virtuous One, you have already fulfilled the ten powers of a Tathāgata and the ten stages (bhūmi); all Buddha-dharmas are entirely complete. For what reason do you not realize unsurpassed bodhi?"
Mañjuśrī said, “Good son, how could there be a further realization of bodhi after having already perfected all the Buddha-dharmas?”
"Why is this? Because it is already perfected, what further could there be to realize? Siṃhavikrama spoke again:
“Mañjuśrī! How does one fulfill all the Buddha-dharmas? He replied:
“Tathatā is perfected. Because Tathatā is perfected, all Buddha-dharmas are perfected; because all Buddha-dharmas are perfected, space is perfected.”
Space, suchness, and all Buddha-dharmas are non-dual and without distinction.

Furthermore, son of good family, regarding what you have said concerning the perfection of the Buddha-dharmas: the perfection of the Buddha-dharmas means the perfection of form, and the perfection of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
“The perfection of the Buddha-dharma is likewise thus. Siṃhavikrama said, “Mañjuśrī!
"What is the perfection of form?
What is the perfection of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Good son! Is the form that you perceive permanent,
or is it impermanent?”
He replied, “No. Mañjuśrī said:
“Good son! If a dharma neither increases nor decreases, it is called ‘perfectly complete. By what causal condition does one know that dharmas are perfectly complete?

When such wisdom is activated, discriminative wisdom arises; if it is not activated, there is no discrimination. There is neither that which is discriminated nor that which performs the discrimination, and thus there is neither increase nor decrease. That which neither increases nor decreases is called ‘equanimity.’”
Therefore, son of good family!

If one perceives the equality of form, that is the perfection of form; if one perceives the equality of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, that is the perfection of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāntagāminirghoṣa addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"You have long since attained the profound patience (*kṣānti*), yet you do not give rise to the thought of forming such an understanding as:
'I have realized awakening (*bodhi*')."
"Now, does Mañjuśrī not desire to awaken sentient beings and encourage them to set their minds on enlightenment?
He replied, "Noble son!..."
I have never awakened sentient beings nor exhorted them.
Why is this? Because sentient beings do not exist, because sentient beings are detached, and because sentient beings are unapprehendable.
If awakening were obtainable, then one would awaken sentient beings and encourage them toward it.
Son of good family!

Since neither I, nor awakening, nor sentient beings can be apprehended, I therefore awaken sentient beings through the encouragement of equality, so that they neither seek supreme awakening nor fall back from it.
Why is this? Because there is no conceptual differentiation, as their nature is equal.
To thoroughly understand that conditioned phenomena neither come nor go is called "equality" and is also termed the "phrase of emptiness."
Regarding the phrase "emptiness," there is nothing to be sought.
Son of good family!
If this is so, how can you say that after a long time one attains patience?
Since there is nothing to be attained, how could I have a mind that realizes bodhi?
Son of good family!
Do you perceive the mind and wisdom as being attained?
He replied, "No. Mañjuśrī said:
"That mind is neither form nor name; yet, up to and including bodhi, it is designated by means of names. Thus, both that bodhi and the mind are not empty, and the names are also not empty."
Sīhavikrānta said: "Good son, do not speak with such intentional ambiguity."
Mañjuśrī said: "Since the mind does not arise, how could I attain bodhi?
Since the mind does not arise, how could there be direct realization?"
Siṃhavikrāmin asked, "What is meant by 'direct realization'? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Good son! To awaken to all phenomena according to their nature and contemplate them as equal is called direct realization;
to thus awaken to them without giving rise to even the slightest notion, nor extinguishing any notion, is called direct realization.”
Thus, when suchness and non-suchness do not give rise to conceptual discrimination, it is called direct realization (*sākṣātkriyā*).

If one abides in right view and is equanimous toward all phenomena because nothing is apprehended, then by means of this non-apprehension—not conceiving of them as one, nor as different, nor thinking of them as one, nor thinking of them as different—it is called direct realization.

If one realizes the single characteristic within the body and knows all phenomena to be what is called "characteristicless," and if one knows all phenomena to be characteristicless, then one will have no defiled attachment to body or mind; this is termed "actualized realization."
“What is meant by ‘attainment’? Mañjuśrī replied, “Noble son!

The phrase "non-practice" is called attainment; one who practices nothing does not move within the three realms, for that which is beyond the three realms cannot be expressed by verbal discourse. Why is this so?
The True Dharma has no ālayavijñāna, nor does it have any sphere of activity; therefore, it cannot be expressed in speech.
Furthermore, son of good family!
There is no verbal expression of sound, nor is there any dharma that can be apprehended; because there is nothing to be apprehended, it is called "attainment."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāntagāminigarjitasvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Excellent!”
"I pray that you will describe the Buddha-field attained by the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī. The Buddha said, "Good son!"
"You should ask the Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta Bodhisattva yourself.
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Siṃhavikrāntagāminigarjitasvara addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"What is the adornment of your noble one's buddha-field?"
He replied, "Good son! If you delight in bodhi, you may ask."
Siṃhavikrāmin asked, "Do you not delight in bodhi? Mañjuśrī replied:
"No, good son! If there is a longing for things, there is aversion; if there is aversion, there is craving; and if there is craving, there is no renunciation."
"Good son! For this reason, I neither take delight in it nor do I feel weary of it.
Furthermore, good son!"
Regarding your question, "How does one accomplish the adornment of a Buddha-field?
I am unable to praise myself. Why is this?
"To speak of the adornments of one’s own buddha-field in the presence of the Tathāgata’s omniscience is for a bodhisattva to praise their own already-accomplished virtues.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
"You should now speak of the adornments of the merits of your own vowed buddha-field."
"Why is this? It is so that all bodhisattvas, having heard it from you, may decisively fulfill this vow. Mañjuśrī said:
"I dare not disobey the Tathāgata’s command; receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, I shall now speak.
At that time, the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, paid homage to the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

I shall now speak; if there are sons or daughters of good family who seek awakening, you should listen attentively. Once you have heard this, it will cause them to fulfill the basis for true practice.
As Mañjuśrī touched his right knee to the ground, in that very instant, the great earth throughout the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, shook in six ways.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I vow that if I do not accumulate the requisites for enlightenment throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, I shall never realize unsurpassed, perfect awakening."
World-Honored One!
With my unimpeded divine eye, I see all the Buddhas throughout the ten directions, even unto immeasurable and boundless worlds.
World-Honored One!

If it were not for my having exhorted them to resolve upon unsurpassed bodhicitta and cultivate the practices of enlightenment, and having exhorted them to study generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, so as to cause them to accomplish the six pāramitās.
Having thus exhorted them, I instructed and admonished them, causing them all to fulfill unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
World-Honored One!
At that time, having observed the ten directions with my unimpeded divine eye and performed the work of a Buddha, I then realized unsurpassed bodhi.
At that time, there were some among the assembly who thought to themselves:
"How is it that the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī has seen such Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones?"
At that time, the Tathāgata, knowing that the bodhisattvas were thinking this, addressed the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāntagāminigarjitasvara, saying: "Good son!
Suppose there were a man who reduced this trichiliocosm into fine particles as small as motes of dust.
What do you think?
Could a mathematician or a mathematician’s disciple calculate and know their number—whether they are hundreds, thousands, koṭis, nayutas, or hundreds of thousands?
"No, World-Honored One! The Buddha said:

“Good son! In this way, the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, observing the ten directions with his unimpeded divine eye, beholds such immeasurable and innumerable Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, in each and every world.”
At that time, Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One! I have such a vow:

"May worlds as vast as the sands of the Ganges become a single buddha-field; may the walls and ramparts within that buddha-field be high and great, reaching to the Peak of Existence, adorned with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of varieties of jewels, further embellished with an interlacing array of countless exquisite gems;
if this is not so, I shall never realize unsurpassed bodhi."
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
I have another vow:
'May the bodhi tree within my land be equal in size to ten thousand great trichiliocosms, and may the radiance of that tree shine universally throughout all Buddha-lands. "
"Furthermore, World-Honored One, I have another vow:

'Having sat beneath the Bodhi tree, from the night I attain equal and perfect enlightenment until the night of my parinirvāṇa, I shall not rise from that seat. Yet, by means of transformation bodies, I shall pervade immeasurable, incalculable koṭis of nayutas of Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions, expounding the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.'"
"Furthermore, World-Honored One! I have another vow:

'May there be no names of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas within my buddha-field; may there be only a pure assembly of great bodhisattvas, free from all faults and afflictions, such that those who practice the pure brahmacarya fill this buddha-field.'"

In that buddha-field, there is not even the name "woman"; all bodhisattvas are born by transformation, wear the saṃghāṭī robes, and sit in the full lotus posture. Such bodhisattvas fill that land, with the sole exception of those emanated by the Tathāgata who travel to the ten directions to teach the Dharma of the three vehicles to sentient beings according to their inclinations.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāntagāminigarjitasvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
When Mañjuśrī attains Buddhahood in the future, what will his name be?"
The Buddha said,
“Good son! When this Mañjuśrī attains Buddhahood, he shall be named Universal Vision (Samantadarśin).”
"Good son! For what reason is that Tathāgata called 'Universal Vision' (Samantadarśin)? Good son!"

Because he universally perceives and causes all beings throughout the immeasurable, incalculable, koṭi-nayuta-hundred-thousand worlds of the ten directions to see him everywhere, he is named Universal Vision (Samantadarśin).
Those sentient beings who see that Buddha will certainly attain unsurpassed enlightenment.

Although the Tathāgata Samantadarśin has not yet attained Buddhahood, if anyone hears his name either during my current lifetime or after my parinirvāṇa, they shall all likewise certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, with the sole exception of those who have already entered the stages of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha, as well as those of inferior resolve.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have yet another vow:”

"Just as in the land of the Tathāgata Amitāyus, one takes the joy of the Dharma as food, so too in my land, when a bodhisattva first gives rise to the thought of eating, bowls filled with food of a hundred flavors immediately appear in their right hand; then, they reflect thus:"

"If I have not made offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions, nor bestowed gifts upon impoverished and suffering sentient beings and those in the realm of hungry ghosts for a thousand years—even those who do not receive so much as a drop of saliva—then until I have generously given to satisfy them, I shall never eat for even a single moment. Having attained the five supernormal powers and great majestic virtue, moving through the air unimpeded like the wind, I shall immediately travel to the infinite and countless Buddha-fields of the ten directions to offer food to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and their assemblies of śrāvakas; I shall also bestow it upon impoverished, suffering sentient beings and those in the realm of hungry ghosts, causing them to be fully satisfied and freed from hunger and thirst. Having thus preached the Dharma to them, I shall return to my own land in a single moment."
"Furthermore, World-Honored One, I have another vow:

'Once I have attained Bodhi, when any bodhisattvas are first born within my land, whatever clothing they require shall appear in their hands according to their thoughts— pure garments suitable for śramaṇas.'"
Once this robe had emerged, he thought to himself:
"If I do not first offer this precious robe to the Buddhas of the ten directions, I ought not to enjoy it myself."
As soon as this thought arose, he immediately traveled to countless worlds, offered these precious robes to the Buddhas, returned to his original location, and then donned them himself.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

In my land, whatever articles of enjoyment the assembly of bodhisattvas possess shall first be offered to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and their assemblies of śrāvakas, before being used by themselves."

Furthermore, may my buddha-field be free from the eight difficult conditions and unwholesome sounds; may all suffering be removed from my buddha-field, and may there be no violation of the pure vows and ethical discipline; and may there be nothing among forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles that is not pleasing to the mind.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāntagajagarjitasvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the name of that world?”
“Where else has the Tathāgata Samantadarśin appeared after attaining Buddhahood?
The Buddha said, “Good son!...”
That Buddha-world is named Fulfillment of Wishes, Accumulation of Purity Free from Dust; that Buddha-field lies in this southern direction, and the Sahā world is also situated within it.
Furthermore, the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have another vow:

'In my buddha-field, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of various jewels shall be accumulated; immeasurable maṇi gems shall reflect one another. All these great treasures shall be such that they are difficult to find or even to see in the buddha-fields of the ten directions. The names of all those accumulated maṇi jewels and so forth could not be fully recounted even in hundreds of thousands of koṭis of years.'"

“World-Honored One! In that world, bodhisattvas who delight in seeing that land as gold will see it appear as gold; those who delight in seeing it as silver will see it appear as silver. Yet, while seeing it as gold, it is never diminished. Those who delight in seeing the various immeasurable jewels—such as vaidūrya, crystal, red pearls, agate, musāragalva, and other gems—will each see them according to their desire with their various characteristics. Furthermore, they shall all see the various fragrances they wish for, including agallochum, tagara, tamālapatra, nāgakesara, and sandalwood. This occurs without any alteration in the characteristics of the jewels in that world.”

In that buddha-field, there is no reliance on the sun, moon, stars, or the light of mani-jewels and fire for illumination; rather, light spontaneously issues from the bodhi trees to provide illumination.

Whatever those bodhisattvas desire or delight in, this light illuminates those hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of worlds such that there is no distinction between day and night; day and night are distinguished by the opening and closing of flowers. It accords with whatever seasons those bodhisattvas find pleasing, responding accordingly, and there is likewise no cold or heat, nor old age, sickness, or death.

If any bodhisattvas, according to their own inclinations, desire to realize awakening, they immediately proceed to other realms, where they exhaust their lifespan in Tuṣita Heaven, descend to be born, and attain perfect enlightenment.

In the sky of that buddha-field, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kinds of music constantly play; although no forms appear, their sounds are heard. Within those musical sounds, there are none associated with attachment or defilement; rather, one hears exclusively the sounds of the perfections, the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, as well as the sounds of the teachings of the various Bodhisattva-piṭakas, all of which are fully audible.

Therein, those bodhisattvas, thirsting with longing for the Buddha, wherever they may walk, sit, or stand, shall see, upon merely thinking of him, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin seated at the foot of the Bodhi tree.

"If there are bodhisattvas who have doubts regarding the Dharma, merely by seeing that Buddha, their nets of doubt will all be severed and they will understand the meaning of the Dharma without waiting for an explanation.
At that time, an assembly of immeasurable koṭis of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas spoke these words with one voice:

"Now this World-Honored One’s name is truly consistent with its meaning; that is to say, his title is 'The Tathāgata Universal Vision. How wonderful it would be to obtain such a supreme benefit as merely hearing his name, let alone being born within that Buddha-field!"

If there are those who hear such a discourse on the Dharma regarding this prophecy, and whose ears receive the name of the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, they shall be said to have personally beheld all the Buddhas as they spoke these words.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said."

"Good son! If there were one who upholds the names of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Tathāgatas, and another who recites the name of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, the latter would possess far greater merit; how much more so for one who recites the name of the Buddha Samantadarśin!"
Why is this? The benefit bestowed upon sentient beings by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Tathāgatas does not equal the benefit performed by Mañjuśrī in a single kalpa.

At that time, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others, raised their voices in unison and proclaimed:
"Homage to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta Bodhisattva! Homage to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Sarvadarśin!"

After the many devas and nāgas had spoken these words, eight hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of sentient beings gave rise to the mind set on unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; immeasurable sentient beings matured their roots of goodness and attained non-retrogression from unexcelled bodhi.
Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have yet another vow:”

"As I behold the infinite, countless, koṭi-nayuta-hundred-thousand Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions, may all the various aspects of the meritorious adornments of their respective Buddha-fields be placed within my single Buddha-field—excepting only those fields adorned for the sake of manifesting transformations for śrāvakas and those worlds of the five turbidities."
"If I were to praise the meritorious adornments of my own buddha-field, I could not finish describing them even in as many *gaṅgā* sands of eons as there are.
World-Honored One!
As for my vows, only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, can know them; no one else can."
The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is! Mañjuśrī!”
"The Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are without limit or obstruction throughout the three periods of time.
At that time, some among the assembly had this thought:
"Is the adornment of the Buddha-field described by Mañjuśrī equal to the land of the Tathāgata Amitāyus?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the mind of that bodhisattva, addressed the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāntagāminigarjitasvara, saying: "Good son!
It is like a man who splits a single hair into a hundred parts and, with one part of that hair, takes a single drop of water from the great ocean. Good son!
“Of that single hair’s tip of water or the waters of the great ocean, which is more?
Siṃhavikrama addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The water on a single hair is small, while the water of the great ocean is vast.
The Buddha said:

“Good son! You should see that the water on a single hair-tip raised by that man is like the meritorious adornments of the buddha-field of Amitāyus Tathāgata, while the remaining waters of the great ocean are like the meritorious adornments of the buddha-field of Samantadarśin Tathāgata.”
At that time, Siṃhavikrama addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
In the past, present, and future, has there ever been such a buddha-field adorned with such meritorious qualities?"
The Buddha replied:
"There is, son of good family!"

To the east, passing from here through eighty koṭis of hundreds of thousands of worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is a buddha-field named *Pranidhānasthitocchraya*. In it dwells a Buddha named *Samantaprabhā-nityabahuguṇasāgararāja Tathāgata*, who currently resides there. The Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable and boundless, and he teaches the Dharma surrounded by an assembly of immeasurable great bodhisattvas.

"Good son! The meritorious adornments of that buddha-field are neither more nor less than those of the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Samantadarśin; therein dwell four bodhisattvas who have donned the armor of non-retrogression and abide in such practice."
“Good son! Those bodhisattvas shall also attain this adornment of the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Samantadarśin. Siṃhavikrama said:

“I only pray that you will speak the names of those bodhisattvas and their dwelling places, as well as describe the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Universal Radiance Constantly Abounding Merit Ocean King; manifest those Buddhas and bodhisattvas for me, so that these bodhisattvas may take up that buddha-field.”
The Buddha said:
"Good sons! Listen attentively; I shall now speak."
"Good son! The first bodhisattva is named Prabhāketu; he resides in the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Aśokaśrī in the eastern direction.
The second bodhisattva is named Jñānottara; he resides in the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Jñānarāja in the southern direction."
The third bodhisattva is named Śāntendriya; he resides in the buddha-field of Tathāgata Prajñākūṭa in the western direction.
The fourth bodhisattva is named Praṇidhijñāna; he resides in the buddha-field of Tathāgata Nārāyaṇa in the northern direction.

At that time, the World-Honored One, through his supernormal power of miraculous travel (*ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna*), manifested the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Universal Radiance Ever-Multitudinous Merit-Ocean King, causing this great assembly to behold that Tathāgata and the host of bodhisattvas, as well as the meritorious adornments of that buddha-field—things never before seen or heard, perfected with inconceivable multitudes of marks. These two worlds were able to see one another, as clearly as if looking at an *āmalaka* fruit held in the palm of one's hand.

That Blessed One, the Tathāgata Samantaprabha-nityabahuguṇasāgararāja, has a body eighty-four thousand *yojanas* in height; his golden radiance is majestic and brilliant, like Sumeru, the king of mountains. Surrounded before and behind by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas whose bodies are forty-two thousand *yojanas* in height, he sits upon a lion throne beneath a bodhi tree adorned with immeasurable merits, traveling to koṭi-nayuta worlds to expound the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"Sons of good family!
Do you see the adornments of merit of that Tathāgata’s buddha-field and his assembly of bodhisattvas?"
Then the great assembly, with one voice and in unison, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Indeed, we have seen it.”
"We shall train ourselves in this bodhisattva practice, just as the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī has practiced; we too shall accomplish such adornment of a buddha-field."

At that time, the World-Honored One smiled with a serene countenance, and from his face he emitted various rays of light—namely, blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, purple, and so forth—which illuminated immeasurable and boundless worlds. Having shone upon them, the lights returned, circled the Buddha three times, and entered the crown of his head.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
by what causes and conditions do you manifest this smile?"
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"By virtue of manifesting the meritorious adornments of that buddha-world,
at that time eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas within this great assembly beheld the magnificent array of that buddha-field as being like the buddha-field of the youth Mañjuśrī."
Within that assembly, there were only sixteen noble beings who, having accomplished the superior resolve, made this vow:
"Just as the land of Mañjuśrī is adorned, may we also become thus."

"Except for these sixteen virtuous men, no others were able to conceive such great vows, desiring to swiftly realize unexcelled bodhi, and seeking a Buddha-land adorned with merits like that of Amitāyus."
Maitreya! Do you see now?

A bodhisattva who has accomplished the altruistic intention (*āśaya*) is able to bring about great benefit; because of that superior intention (*adhyāśaya*), they have made this supreme vow, and for this reason, they shall obtain a buddha-field such as that of Mañjuśrī.

Those bodhisattvas who possess little faith and inferior aspirations, due to their feeble karma, must pass through sixty quadrillion (*koṭi-nayuta-śata-sahasra*) kalpas before they finally fulfill the five *pāramitās*.

At that time, four great bodhisattvas—Prabhāketu, Jñānottara, Śāntendriya, and Praṇidhijñāna—came from the four directions and appeared there. Each sat within a pavilion of immeasurable vaidūrya light, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of devas. They caused all the buddha-fields to tremble and, through various supernormal powers, scattered hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of flowers and played celestial music.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what causes and conditions does this world experience such a great earthquake?”
“Furthermore, four multi-storied pavilions have appeared in the four directions?
The Buddha said, “Maitreya!”
"These four bodhisattvas have come to pay their respects to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, having been alerted by the Buddha.

Before he had finished speaking, in that very instant, these four bodhisattvas descended from the pavilion, approached the Buddha, prostrated themselves at his feet, circumambulated him three times, and withdrew to sit to one side; the radiance of those bodhisattvas came from the four directions, illuminating the entire assembly.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"Sons of good family!
These four right-minded ones abide in an inconceivable purpose. You should conceive a heart of extraordinary reverence toward these right-minded ones and inquire about the essentials of the Dharma."
"Good sons! You should listen to the vow of that noble being. That which is the vow of that noble being is the entirety of the Bodhisattva Vehicle. Good sons!"
"O virtuous woman!

If there are those who behold those four bodhisattvas, they shall attain non-retrogression in unsurpassed bodhi, transcend twenty koṭis of kalpas of wandering in birth and death, and become fully perfected in the five pāramitās."
"If any woman hears his name, she shall quickly attain liberation from the female body.
At that time, the World-Honored One withdrew the miraculous power after manifesting that land, and that world suddenly vanished.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
All dharmas are like illusions; they are like the illusory feats created by a magician, which appear as illusions and then vanish again."
"World-Honored One!
Thus all dharmas, having arisen, again perish; yet they are also without arising or perishing—this is equality.
World-Honored One!"
"If one trains in equality, one will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Jñānottara addressed the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"In what way does one realize unsurpassed enlightenment?"
Mañjuśrī said: "Good son! Dharmas are neither to be attained nor to be destroyed;
one has no attachment to non-existence, and there is nothing to be attained within existence."
The Bodhisattva Jñānottara said:
“Mañjuśrī! Is bodhi attained because of existence?”
"Or is it for the sake of non-existence? He replied, "Good son!"
“Dharmas are fundamentally unarisen; they have not existed in the past, do not exist in the present, and will not exist in the future;
ultimately, nothing can be apprehended. Bodhisattva Jñānottara said, “Mañjuśrī!
"By what single characteristic do you teach the Dharma? Mañjuśrī replied, "Good son!"
"What is the single-characterized Dharma that you speak of? Bodhisattva Jñānottara replied, "Mañjuśrī!..."

One does not perceive the aggregates, the sense bases, or the elements; nor is there the view of non-existence, nor the view of existence. One has no conceptualization regarding phenomena, nor anything to be conceptualized. Furthermore, one does not perceive phenomena as accumulating, nor does one perceive them as dispersing. This is called the Dharma-gate of the Single Characteristic.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāntagajagarjitasvara said:

“If one does not contravene the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) regarding the nature of phenomena, and does not engage in various conceptual discriminations—such as ‘this is the dharma of ordinary beings,’ ‘this is the dharma of śrāvakas,’ ‘this is the dharma of pratyekabuddhas,’ or ‘this is the dharma of Tathāgatas’—but enters into the single characteristic, namely the characteristic of detachment, this is precisely what is called the Dharma-gate of the Single Characteristic.”
The Bodhisattva Priyadarśana said:
“If one practices suchness while having no conceptualization of suchness, nor discriminating that ‘this is profound,’ this is called the Dharma-gate of the Single Characteristic.”
The Bodhisattva Akṣayapratibhāna said:

“All dharmas are exhausted; that which is ultimately exhausted is called inexhaustible. To speak of all dharmas as being inexhaustible is precisely what is named the Dharma-gate of the Single Characteristic.”
The Bodhisattva Subhāvitacitta said:
"If one enters non-thought through thought, there is nothing to be thought of, nor is anything to be apprehended; this is precisely what is called the Dharma-gate of the Single Characteristic."
The Bodhisattva Free from Dust said:

"If one is ultimately unstained regarding all marks, such that there is no staining even in what is stained, and one is without attachment, aversion, or delusion; neither creating unity nor creating difference, neither acting nor not acting, neither grasping nor abandoning—this is precisely what is called the Dharma-gate of the Single Mark."
The Bodhisattva Sāketa said:

"If one enters the profound Dharma, which is as difficult to fathom as the great ocean, yet does not engage in conceptual discrimination regarding the True Dharma—abiding thus and speaking thus, having no thoughts of one's own and nothing to speak to others—this is called the Dharma-gate of the Single Characteristic."
The Bodhisattva Candrottara-kumārabhūta said:

"If one contemplates all sentient beings as being equal to the moon, yet does not conceive of a self or of sentient beings, to speak in this way is precisely what is called the Dharma-gate of the Single Characteristic."
The Bodhisattva Destroyer of All Sorrow and Darkness said:
"If one encounters sorrow and grief yet remains without anxiety, and does not grow weary even by the arrows of sorrow, how could sentient beings give rise to the faculty of sorrow?"
"What is called 'abiding in equanimity toward whatever exists in relation to the self' is precisely what is termed the Dharma-gate of the Single Characteristic.
The Bodhisattva Anālambana said:

"If one does not take the desire realm as an object, does not take the form or formless realms as objects, does not take the dharmas of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas as objects, and does not take the Buddha-dharmas as objects—to speak in this way is precisely what is termed the Dharma-gate of the Single Characteristic."
The Bodhisattva Samantadarśin said:

“One who preaches the Dharma should preach with equanimity. That which is equanimous is what is called emptiness. One does not contemplate equanimity within emptiness, nor is there anything to be attained within the dharma of equanimity.
To preach in this manner is precisely what is called the Dharma-gate of the Single Characteristic.”
The Bodhisattva Pure in the Three Spheres said:
"The Dharma that is taught does not contradict the three spheres. What are these three? They are: the sphere of the speaker, the sphere of the listener, and the sphere of the teaching."
To have nothing attained regarding the self, no conceptualization regarding what is heard, and no grasping regarding phenomena—
this is called the purity of the three spheres.
That which is thus described is precisely what is called the Dharma-gate of the Single Characteristic.
The Bodhisattva Accomplished Practice said:
"If one knows that all phenomena are without attachment, and thus knows and thus speaks— yet does not speak even a single word, because they are free from verbal expression—
and if one speaks of all phenomena in this manner, this is precisely what is called the Dharma-gate of the Single Characteristic."
The Bodhisattva Profound Practice said:

"If one delights in yoga and knows all dharmas, then one perceives nothing within those dharmas. Whether one speaks of them or does not speak of them, there is no duality regarding dharmas; this is precisely what is called the Dharma-gate of the Single Characteristic."
In this manner, these immeasurable bodhisattvas of great majesty and virtue each, by means of their own eloquence, expounded the Dharma of the Single Characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇadharma*).

While this Dharma-gate of the Single Characteristic was being taught, seventy *koṭi* of bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*); eighty thousand *nayuta* of hundreds of thousands of sentient beings resolved their minds upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (*anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi*); seven thousand bhikṣus exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*) and attained liberation of mind; and ninety-six *nayuta* of humans and devas attained the pure Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣurviśuddhi*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Siṃhavikrāntagāminigarjitasvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How many great bodhisattvas constitute the retinue of that Tathāgata Samantadarśin?”
"What will his lifespan be?
After how much time will Mañjuśrī attain equal and perfect enlightenment?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! You should ask the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī about this matter.
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Siṃhavikrāntagāminirghoṣa addressed the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"How much time will it be before you attain bodhi? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O son of good family!..."
If the realm of empty space were to take on the form of physical matter, only then would I realize unsurpassed bodhi;
if a man conjured by a magician were to realize bodhi, only then would I realize unsurpassed bodhi;
if an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted were to realize bodhi, only then would I realize unsurpassed bodhi.
If a man in a dream, or a reflection, or an echo, were thus to manifest as a transformation and realize awakening;
or if I were to realize unsurpassed awakening;
or if the light of the sun were to become night and the light of the moon were to become day—only then would I realize unsurpassed awakening.
"Noble son! You may now question those who seek awakening. Siṃhavikrama said:
“Mañjuśrī, do you not seek bodhi? He replied, “Virtuous man!
"No. Why is this? Mañjuśrī is himself bodhi, and bodhi is itself Mañjuśrī."
Why is this? There are only names, and names are also empty.
From Mañjuśrī up to bodhi, even the name is far removed; it is non-existent and empty, and that which is empty is itself bodhi.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāntaghoṣa, saying:
"Have you ever seen or heard of the assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas of the Tathāgata Amitāyus?"
“Yes, World-Honored One! I have indeed seen and heard it. “Good son!”
"What do you think? He replied,
"It is beyond the reach of calculation or conceptual thought."
The Buddha said, “Good son!

Suppose there were one *vāha* of sesame seeds in the kingdom of Magadha; taking a single seed as a metaphor for the assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas in the land of Amitāyus, you should understand that the assembly of bodhisattvas when the bodhisattva Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta attains enlightenment is even more so. You should know it in this way.”

"Good son! Suppose one were to grind the trichiliocosm into fine dust, and let each particle of dust represent one kalpa; compared to the number of kalpas in the lifespan of the Tathāgata Samantadarśin, this would not even approach a hundredth part, a thousandth part, a hundred-thousandth part, or a koṭi-th part—it would be beyond the reach of calculation or analogy."
"Good son! By means of calculation, reckoning, and measurement, you should know that the lifespan of the Tathāgata Samantadarśin is immeasurable and boundless. Good son!"

Suppose, for example, that the trichiliocosm were reduced to atoms of dust. A certain man were to take one atom, or even many atoms, and after passing beyond a trichiliocosm, drop a single atom; that man proceeds eastward in this manner until all the atoms have been dropped. In the same way, each of the men in the ten directions acts according to the previous example until all those atoms have been dropped.
"Good son! What do you think?
Regarding that trichiliocosm—whether it be a hundred, a thousand, or hundreds of thousands of koṭis and nayutas—do you know its measure?"
He replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
“Good son! Suppose these ten men each take a mote of dust from a trichiliocosm and cast it down.
All those worlds—those already cast upon and those yet to be cast—would be entirely ground into dust.”
"Good son! What do you think?
Could one possibly calculate whether these are hundreds, thousands, or hundreds of thousands of koṭis and nayutas?"
He replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said:

"Good son! Suppose there were ten men from each of the ten directions who, having traversed beyond a trichiliocosm, took the atoms they had dropped as well as the places where they had not dropped any, and ground them all into dust."
"Good son! What do you think?
Could one possibly calculate those atoms—whether they be hundreds, thousands, koṭis, nayutas, hundreds of thousands, or even up to an ayuta, a nimbara, or an akṣobhya?"
“World-Honored One!
If a person hears this calculation, their mind will become bewildered; its quantity cannot be known.
The Buddha said:
“Good son! The Tathāgata fully knows those atoms—whether they be hundreds, thousands, koṭis, nayutas, hundreds of thousands, or even up to ayutas, vivaras, akṣobhyas, and so forth.”
"Good son! Thus the Tathāgata knows them all, and even exceeds that measure.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there is a bodhisattva who seeks such inexhaustible wisdom that realizes the nature of form, would they not rather undergo the suffering of hell for immeasurable kalpas, yet never abandon this great wisdom regarding form?”
The Buddha said: “Maitreya! So it is, so it is!”
It is as you have said.
How could anyone fail to give rise to aspiration toward the Buddha’s inexhaustible great wisdom,
except for those of inferior resolve and the indolent?
When these words regarding the Great Wisdom of the Tathāgata were spoken, ten thousand sentient beings gave rise to the bodhicitta.
The Buddha addressed Siṃhavikrama, saying:
"O son of good family!
"In this way, O son of good family, after as many eons as there are atoms in the worlds of the ten directions, and as many atoms as were placed beneath those ten men, [he will attain it]."
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta has manifested the practice of the bodhisattva path throughout many eons. Why is this?
O son of good family!
Mañjuśrī is inconceivable; his vows are inconceivable; his approach is inconceivable;
having realized bodhi, his lifespan is inconceivable, and his assembly of bodhisattvas is also inconceivable.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Siṃhavikrāntagāminigarjitasvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How rare! How extraordinary!”
Mañjuśrī’s resolve is exceedingly great, and his practice is vast:
namely, that the youthful Mañjuśrī does not give rise to weariness throughout as many eons as there are atoms in those [lands].
Mañjuśrī said: "Good son, what do you think?"
Does space have such thoughts regarding day and night, half-months, months, seasons, years, kalpas, hundreds of kalpas, thousands of kalpas, or hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas?
He replied, "No, Mañjuśrī!"
"Why is this? Because the realm of space is without discrimination. Mañjuśrī said:

“Good son! If one awakens to all phenomena as being equal to space, then in accordance with that awakening, one does not engage in conceptualization; there is no conceptualization whatsoever. Regarding those days and nights, half-months, months, seasons, years, and so forth, as previously explained, there arises not even the slightest notion regarding phenomena.”

"Good son! Just as when a great fire blazes within the realm of space for immeasurable kalpas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the realm of space never arises, nor is it ever burned or destroyed."
Why is this? Because the realm of empty space has no intrinsic nature.
Thus it is, son of good family!

If a bodhisattva knows that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature, they likewise experience no feverish distress or weariness; like space, which is neither burned nor subject to weariness or distress, they remain unshakable—neither arising, nor decaying, nor dying, nor migrating, nor originating, and without going or coming.
"So it is, so it is! Son of good family, the name Mañjuśrī is likewise:
it is neither burned nor destroyed, neither weary nor afflicted by heat, neither shaken nor moved; it is unborn, imperishable, deathless, non-transmigrating, unarisen, and without going or coming."
Why is this? Because names are ultimately and utterly remote.

When this Dharma was being spoken, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, Śakra Devānām Indra, Mahābrahmā, and other sons of gods of great majesty and virtue, with one voice and in unison, proclaimed these words:
"If sentient beings obtain such great and virtuous benefit merely by hearing this Dharma-gate, how much more so by receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting it?
You should know that it cannot be accomplished through meager roots of goodness."
“World-Honored One!
We shall receive, uphold, read, recite, and widely propagate this Dharma-gate for the sake of protecting and maintaining the True Dharma.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāntagāminigarjitasvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If good men and good women receive, uphold, read, and recite this Dharma-gate, and for the sake of others proclaim such essential teachings, the accomplishment of the adornments of Buddha-fields, and give rise to such a mind—just as Mañjuśrī has done—how much merit will they obtain?”
The Buddha said, “Good son!

As for the worlds seen by the Tathāgata with his unobstructed eye, if there were a bodhisattva who filled those worlds with the seven precious treasures and offered them as gifts to each and every Buddha, continuing such renunciation and giving throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges until the end of the future, this would cause that bodhisattva to abide securely in the discipline of pure precepts and attain a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.”

If there is a bodhisattva who upholds, recites, and studies this Dharma-gate of the Merit-Adornment of this Buddha-field, and furthermore resolves to follow the training of Mañjuśrī, then compared to the previous mass of merit, the mass of merit from seven steps cannot be reached by even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, a *kalā* part, a hundred-thousandth part, or a *koṭi*-thousandth part; indeed, it is beyond the reach of calculation.

At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva entered the bodhisattva samādhi called "Equal Illumination of the Illusory Nature. Having entered it, by virtue of Mañjuśrī’s samādhi, even the assembly of bodhisattvas and others perceived nearby the infinite and boundless Buddha-worlds of the ten directions; before each and every Buddha, there was a Mañjuśrī preaching upon the meritorious adornments of his own buddha-field.

Having seen this, the assembly was struck with wonder at the wisdom of Mañjuśrī’s Samādhi of Supreme Vows; they thought, "May we all behold Mañjuśrī, the youthful Bodhisattva, the son of the Dharma King, amidst hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
what should this Dharma-gate be named?"
"How should it be received and upheld?
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"This Dharma-gate is named 'The Play of All Buddhas'; you should receive and uphold it."
It is also titled "Inconceivable Vows," which you should uphold;
it is also titled "Expounding the Meritorious Adornments of Buddha-fields," which you should uphold;
it is also titled "Arousing Bodhicitta and Inspiring Joy," which you should reverently uphold.

At that time, the immeasurable assembly of bodhisattvas gathered from the ten directions made a great offering to the Buddha and the Dharma. They rained down various celestial flowers, prostrated with their heads at his feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and each returned to their own land, uttering these words of praise:
"How marvelous!"
World-Honored One!
How marvelous!
World-Honored One!
"May we hear this inconceivable Dharma and the great lion’s roar of the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī.

Having spoken these words, bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges attained non-retrogression from unsurpassed enlightenment, and immeasurable sentient beings brought their roots of virtue to fulfillment.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the youth Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Siṃhavikrāntagāminigarjitasvara, all the great Śrāvakas, Brahmā, Śakra, the World Protectors, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others, were all greatly rejoiced, and they faithfully accepted and practiced it.
